CM: Agreed, and let's kill the other rumour right now. I never told Rosa that Uma dropped Dmitri. I told Rosa that Uma had 'processed a withdrawal for one of the Delgados' and Rosa, with respect, you filled in the rest yourself.

RP: That... is unfortunately accurate. Moving on before I die of embarrassment.

CM: Item two, the hardship refund. Dmitri wants a partial lab-fee refund under the hardship clause. The handbook says hardship refunds apply when a student withdraws for documented work-schedule changes within the first 8 weeks. We're in week 6, he attached his Kestrel Dental rota, so handbooks says yes. HOWEVER -- and I checked with Callum by phone, he agreed -- the autumn Python pre-enrolment discount Dmitri received includes a signed waiver saying he accepts no lab-fee refunds on any withdrawal. So the waiver beats the hardship clause. Decision: no refund. We WILL waive his 25-pound late-withdrawal admin fee as a goodwill gesture, that's approved, effective today.

UK: Minuted. Also flag: Antonia Delgado got a 'sorry to see you go' email meant for Dmitri, because the roster system matched on surname. She's fine, she thought it was funny, but let's fix the template.

CM: Noted, action on IT. Item three, the Saturday double-booking. Rosa, walk us through it.

RP: So, the mix-up. I double-booked the entire Saturday cohort -- Kestrel Dental's oral-health workshop AND the exam prep session in the same room at the same time, 11am Saturday. My fault, the calendar migrated badly, whatever, it's on me. And Chiara, I want to say, brilliant job on the catering numbers for that Saturday, truly, you ordering sandwiches for the exam-prep headcount while I'd booked the workshop headcount with Copperleaf has created the single most confusing invoice I have ever seen.

CM: Was that sarcasm, Rosa?

RP: Yes. Obviously. I'm drowning here.

CM: Decision time on item three, people, actual decisions: (1) We EXTEND Dmitri's autumn Python payment deadline by two weeks, he asked in his form and it costs us nothing -- approved. (2) The Kestrel Dental workshop on Saturday is CANCELLED, I phoned their practice manager this morning and confirmed, we'll reschedule for June -- approved, done. (3) Rosa's proposal to hire Callum Sorensen as a paid weekend tutor to cover the reschedule -- I'm shelving that one, Callum's got a conflict of interest since he negotiated the Granite storage contract, we'll use agency staff instead, sorry Rosa. So: extended deadline, yes; cancelled workshop, yes; hire Callum, no; cancel exam prep, no; lab-fee refund, no; late-fee waiver, yes. That's the whole slate. Anyone got anything else?

CM: Minuted. Meeting closed 3:40pm. These minutes to be circulated, and Rosa, don't paraphrase me again please.

P.S. from Uma, written 5pm: also, in case anyone asks, I did NOT initiate Dmitri's withdrawal, and I did not process one for Antonia either -- she's still enrolled, she's fine, she's actually thriving. Then attached: EMAIL THREAD re Viktor leave, MEETING NOTES re handbook review, CHAT LOG re coverage july


SECTION A. REMOTE & HYBRID WORK

A.1 Who can work remote.
Everyone full time can work remote up to 3 days per week (Mon–Fri). Part time folks get 1 day. Interns get none, sorry, come enjoy the office popcorn machine.

A.2 Which days.
Team leads pick anchor days. Anchor day = day everybody must be in office. Most teams anchor is Tuesday. Sales anchors Tuesday AND Thursday because customers like a full house. If you dont know your anchor day, ask your lead, do not guess, guessing caused problems before.

A.3 Hotelling.
We got rid of assigned desks in the Portland office in 2023. You book a desk thru the FoxDesk app. Book by 5pm the day before. If you book and no-show 3 times in one month, app locks you out for 2 weeks and you sit in the lunch room which honestly has better chairs anyway.

A.4 Remote outside Oregon.
Working remote from another state for more than 14 days total in a calendar year requires a form. Form is HR-402. Nobody ever fills this out, please start. Tax people are getting nervous. Working from another COUNTRY requires HR-402 plus legal sign off and minimum 30 days notice. Working from the moon is not addressable under current policy.

A.5 Internet.
You need internet that works. If your internet drops during a client call twice in a week, lead can pull your remote days for that month. This is not a punishment, its a coverage thing. The company does NOT pay your home internet bill. The company DOES pay for a headset, see Section D.

A.6 Timezones.
Core hours are 9:30–3:00 Pacific. If you live in a timezone more than 3 hours off, you and your lead set written core overlap hours. Written means in the HRIS notes field, not a handshake.

A.7 Dress code (current).
Business casual in office. On camera for client calls: top half business casual, whatever below. Hoodies fine on non-client days. Sandals fine year round. This section is under review, see meeting notes attached.

A.8 Remote day tracking.
Remote days are tracked automatically by badge absence. If you badge in and leave after lunch, that still counts as office day, the system is not smart. If you work from home while sick, log it as sick day not remote day, its not a vacation.

A.9 Grandfathered exceptions.
Employees hired before 2022 who had written remote arrangements keep them until role change. Currently 4 people are grandfathered: (names on file with HR, not in this doc for privacy, which defeats the purpose of a policy doc, noted for rev 8).

A.10 Contractors.
Not covered by this section. Contractors follow their own contracts. Stop emailing HR about contractors, please.


SECTION B. TIME OFF: PTO, PARENTAL LEAVE, SABBATICAL

B.1 PTO.
Full time employees accrue PTO at 15 days/year for years 0–2, 20 days for years 3–7, 25 days for 8+. Accrual per paycheck, you can borrow up to 5 unaccrued days with lead approval. PTO requests over 5 consecutive business days need 30 days advance notice in the HRIS. Under 5 days, one week notice is polite but the rule is 3 business days.

B.2 PTO carryover.
Max carryover 5 days into the new calendar year. Rest forfeits. Yes forfeits, we warned you in October, we put it in the November newsletter, Ines made a meme about it.

B.3 Blackout windows.
Fulfillment: Nov 15–Dec 20. Support: none, support takes turns. Sales: first week of each quarter unless quota already hit.

B.4 Parental leave.
All new parents (birth, adoption, foster placement, surrogacy) get 8 weeks paid parental leave at 100% of base pay. Runs within 12 months of the birth/placement date. Can be split into 2 chunks minimum 2 weeks each. Both parents eligible if both work here. Request via HRIS at least 21 days before intended start if foreseeable. HR confirmation required — leave is not considered approved until the HR status shows APPROVED. Approvals are signed by the People Ops Director. Start date can be moved once by the employee without a new request, moved twice = new request.

B.5 Sabbatical.
After 7 continuous years of service, employees are eligible to apply for a 4-week paid sabbatical, one per lifetime at this company. Apply in Q1 for same-year sabbaticals; the company approves up to 2 per year. Applications reviewed by People Ops Director. If denied, you can reapply next year, no hard feelings, capacity reasons.

B.6 Sick days.
10 sick days/year, separate from PTO. Sick days dont carry over, dont pay out. If you are sick more than 3 consecutive days, HR may ask for a doctors note. We hate asking, blame the auditors.

B.7 Bereavement.
5 days for immediate family (spouse/domestic partner, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, plus spouse's parents and siblings). 2 days for aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, close friends, step relations. 1 day if you need to travel 500+ miles for any of the above, added on top. Definitions under review, see meeting notes attached.

B.8 Jury duty & voting.
Jury duty: paid difference between jury pay and normal pay, unlimited. Voting: early voting exists, use PTO if you want a whole day, otherwise polls are open after work.

B.9 Unpaid leave.
Up to 90 days unpaid leave with Director approval, benefits continue. Beyond 90 days benefits stop unless COBRA.

B.10 Returning from leave.
Same or equivalent role guaranteed for parental leave and sick leave. For sabbatical, same role guaranteed. For unpaid leave, equivalent role guaranteed. Schedule a return-to-work chat with HR the week before you come back, bring snacks, optional.


SECTION C. TUITION & PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT REIMBURSEMENT

C.1 What counts.
Job-related courses, certifications, workshops, one conference per year, books yes if job related, podcast subscriptions no, a standing desk treadmill no.

C.2 Caps.
Undergraduate or certification programs: $2,000 per employee per calendar year. Graduate programs: $3,500 per year. One conference per year: registration + travel up to $1,800 combined. Books/materials: $300 per year, inside or outside the tuition cap? Outside, its a separate line, dont get clever.

C.3 Grades.
For graded courses, need B or better for full reimbursement, C gets 50%, below C gets zero. Pass/fail courses need the pass. Certifications need the actual cert copy, not a screenshot of the score page, we been burned.

C.4 How to request.
Submit BEFORE enrolling using HR-311. Pre-approval is required. Retroactive requests considered case by case but default is no. HR has 10 business days to respond, silence is not approval, silence is silence.

C.5 Repayment clawback.
If you leave the company within 12 months of a reimbursement over $1,000, you repay 50% of it. Prorated by month. Payroll deducts it from final checks if needed.

C.6 What never counts.
Anything unrelated to your role or a plausible next role at Foxglove. Someone tried to expense a scuba certification because we sell rain jackets. Denied. HR laughed, then felt bad, then denied again.


SECTION D. EQUIPMENT & EXPENSES

D.1 New hire kit: laptop, monitor if requested, headset, mouse. All company property.
D.2 Replacement: broken equipment swapped free, lost equipment is $150 deductible per item unless police report.
D.3 Expense reports: submit within 30 days of purchase, itemized, receipts over $25. Mileage at IRS rate.
D.4 Office snacks: free. Coffee: free but the good beans only on Fridays, dont fight about it.


SECTION E. COMPLAINTS & DISPUTES

E.1 Disagreements about any of the above go first to your lead, then People Ops, then the skip-level. E.2 Everything above is policy and binding. E.3 This pack supersedes the handbook v4 where they conflict, except the payroll sections, the handbook still owns payroll. E.4 If you find a typo that changes a meaning, tell Uma, there are typos, there are always typos.

FOXGLOVE HEALTH — DEVELOPER PORTAL FAQ (excerpt, last reviewed 3 March 2025)
Maintained by the Developer Experience group. Entries below are reproduced verbatim from the patient-data integration FAQ. This page covers questions we receive about the Foxglove Health data API, the reporting CLI, and webhook configuration. It does not cover billing; see the separate billing FAQ.

────────────────────────────────
Q1. How do I get access to the patient-data API?
A1. Access to the patient-data API requires a server-side API key issued per environment. Client-side keys (browser keys) are never valid for patient-data endpoints, even read-only ones. To obtain a server-side key, your organization's Foxglove contact person submits the key request form on the portal; individual developers cannot self-issue keys. Keys rotate every 90 days and the old key remains valid for 24 hours after rotation as a grace overlap.

────────────────────────────────
Q2. Can I use the same key in staging and production?
A2. No. Keys are environment-bound. A staging key used against production endpoints receives HTTP 403 with error code FOX-ENV-MISMATCH. This is the single most common support ticket we receive, so we mention it here at the top of the page.

────────────────────────────────
Q3. What happens if my key expires during a batch job?
A3. Batch jobs should implement the renewal handshake: 15 minutes before expiry the API returns an X-Renew-Soon header on every response, and your job should request a refreshed key via the /key/renew endpoint using the current key. Jobs that ignore the header will receive HTTP 401 once expiry passes, and HTTP 401 responses are not retried automatically by the gateway.

────────────────────────────────
Q4. How are webhooks secured?
A4. Every webhook payload is signed with an HMAC-SHA256 signature placed in the X-Fox-Signature header. Your receiver must verify the signature using the shared secret shown in the portal under Integrations > Webhooks. Payloads without a valid signature must be rejected by your side. Note that the signature covers the raw request body, not the parsed JSON, so verification must happen before any re-serialization. We recommend verifying before parsing, because re-serializing the JSON and signing that will produce a different byte sequence and the check will fail.

────────────────────────────────
Q5. What is the webhook delivery timeout, and what happens when a delivery times out?
A5. The gateway waits up to 10 seconds for your endpoint to acknowledge with a 2xx status. On timeout the connection is closed and the delivery attempt is recorded with status 'timeout'. You can see attempt logs under Integrations > Webhooks > Delivery log. The delivery log shows the timestamp of each attempt and the response code, when one was received.

────────────────────────────────
Q6. Which HTTP status codes should my webhook endpoint return?
A6. Any 2xx code marks the delivery as acknowledged. Codes 3xx are treated as failures because the gateway does not follow redirects. Codes 4xx and 5xx are treated as failures and logged with the code received.

────────────────────────────────
Q7. How do I export nightly ward reports with the CLI?
A7. The reporting CLI (fh-report) supports the command 'fh-report ward nightly' with flags --date and --format (csv|json). By default it writes to the current directory. Authentication for the CLI uses the same server-side key as the API, supplied via the FOX_KEY environment variable. The CLI does not support browser keys.

────────────────────────────────
Q8. Is the old legacy CLI still supported?
A8. The legacy CLI (fh-legacy) is in maintenance mode: it still runs and will keep running for the foreseeable future, but new features land only in fh-report. Removal of fh-legacy is scheduled in principle, however no removal date has been announced yet, and we will give at least 90 days notice on this page before it stops working. Do not migrate based on rumors in community channels.

────────────────────────────────
Q9. Are there rate limits on the patient-data API?
A9. Yes: 600 requests per minute per key, and 60 requests per second per key, both enforced. Exceeding either limit returns HTTP 429 with the limit that was hit named in the response body. The response also carries a Retry-After header expressed in whole seconds. Bursts up to 50 requests are allowed to arrive simultaneously without tripping the per-second limit, provided the rolling average stays under the per-second value.

────────────────────────────────
Q10. Where can I ask a question that is not on this page?
A10. Write to devex@foxglovehealth.example. Please include the environment, the endpoint, and the correlation ID from the response header X-Fox-Correlation. Questions about pricing or invoices sent to this address are forwarded to the billing team, which maintains a separate FAQ; we cannot answer billing questions ourselves.

────────────────────────────────
PORTAL FOOTER: This FAQ is generated from an internal knowledge base. Sections are reviewed quarterly. Last review: 3 March 2025. Next scheduled review: June 2025. If you notice an inconsistency between this page and the API behavior, the API behavior is authoritative for technical matters, and the master integration agreement is authoritative for commercial matters.

They must not be quoted to customers. The retry policy for webhooks is currently undefined; a future release note will define it.

THISTLE ANALYTICS — INTERNAL ENGINEERING REPORT
Report TR-2025-07: Migration of build infrastructure from Jenkins to the hosted CI platform
Author: Wanjiru Delgado, Senior Infrastructure Engineer
Peer reviewer: Farid Bergstrom, Staff Engineer
Date of report: 30 June 2025
Status: FINAL (with appended post-mortem addendum added 15 July 2025)
Distribution: Platform Engineering leadership, Finance Business Partner

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The migration of Thistle Analytics' build infrastructure from the self-hosted Jenkins estate to the hosted CI platform was proposed in January 2025 with an original completion target of 31 May 2025. This report summarizes the outcome. In the executive view presented to leadership on 2 June, the migration was described as on track; the fuller picture, including schedule performance, cost performance and the incidents in Appendix C, is set out below. Readers who only need the headline numbers should read Section 2 and the Addendum.

2. SCOPE AND DELIVERABLES
The scope covered 43 build pipelines across four teams: data-ingest, model-training, reporting and mobile. Deliverables were: (a) all pipelines reproducible on the hosted platform, (b) build times within 10% of the Jenkins baseline, (c) monthly infrastructure cost at or below $8,000, and (d) a rollback runbook per pipeline. All 43 pipelines were migrated. However, as detailed in Appendix B, the mobile team's four pipelines were migrated in a degraded mode: they build successfully, but artifact signing is still performed by the old Jenkins signing node, which was therefore kept alive outside the original plan.

3. SCHEDULE PERFORMANCE (BODY OF REPORT, AS WRITTEN ON 30 JUNE)
At the time of writing, we assess the schedule as broadly on track. The original target date of 31 May was ambitious, and the final cutover for the data-ingest team was completed on 30 May. The mobile signing exception is a small residual. We do not consider the migration late in any material sense.

4. COST PERFORMANCE
The business case (approved 12 January 2025) projected annual run-cost savings of $18,000 versus the Jenkins estate, based on retiring eight build VMs. During the migration quarter we measured actual run-cost savings of $11,400 over three months, which annualizes to roughly $45,600. We are therefore ahead of plan on cost. Finance has reviewed these figures in draft. NOTE FROM FINANCE BUSINESS PARTNER (added in review, 8 July): the three-month figure above was measured before the May overage invoices arrived; see Addendum, Section A.4, for the corrected figures, which are the ones Finance will use.

5. TEAM FEEDBACK
Quotes collected from engineers in June:
- "The new platform is a genuine improvement, the cache alone saved us hours." (model-training engineer)
- "Mostly better. The mobile signing situation is a bit awkward and nobody documented it until now." (mobile engineer)
- "I would not go back to Jenkins." (reporting engineer)
One engineer left the company in May and did not respond to the feedback survey; their view is not represented.

6. RECOMMENDATIONS (BODY, 30 JUNE)
R1. Declare the migration complete and disband the migration working group.
R2. Decommission the remaining Jenkins signing node once mobile signing is re-implemented on the hosted platform (owner: mobile team, no date committed).
R3. Keep the Jenkins estate powered on until 31 August as a safety net.

ADDENDUM — POST-MORTEM, ADDED 15 JULY 2025 AFTER FINANCE REVIEW AND THE 14 JULY INCIDENT REVIEW MEETING
Minutes and corrections follow. Where the addendum contradicts the body of the report, the addendum is authoritative.

A.1 SCHEDULE CORRECTION. The 30 June claim of 'broadly on track' was too generous. The original completion target was 31 May. The signing work for mobile pipelines (scope item d, arguably also item a) was not finished on 30 June and, as of 14 July, still is not finished. R2 in the body committed to no date. The incident review meeting therefore ruled the migration INCOMPLETE against the original target; the schedule slipped past 31 May with no revised date on file. Wanjiru Delgado accepted this correction in the meeting. Farid Bergstrom, who reviewed the body of the report, stated he had flagged the wording before publication but the flag was not incorporated.

A.2 INCIDENTS (Appendix C material). Two production-relevant incidents occurred during the migration window and were not included in the body of the report:
  Incident 2025-06-11: a mis-translated Jenkins credential path caused the reporting pipeline to publish an unsigned container image to the internal registry for six hours before detection. Risk type: security/compliance.
  Incident 2025-06-19: hosted platform cache eviction logic purged warm caches for model-training three times in one week, extending the median build time from 14 minutes to 41 minutes, above the 10% tolerance in scope item (b) for that week. Risk type: performance.
A third issue, the Jenkins signing node remaining alive with unpatched OS (risk type: security), is considered by the meeting to be an open risk but NOT an incident that materialized during the window, because no exploit or outage occurred.

A.3 COST CORRECTION. After the May overage invoices arrived, Finance recomputed: actual measured savings over the three-month window were $6,200, not $11,400, because two months carried overage charges from burst capacity during cache incidents. Annualized, Finance does not project $45,600; it projects $24,800, still above the business case, but the quarterly figure to report is $6,200. The business case figure of $18,000 annual savings remains the reference: actual annualized savings of $24,800 exceed it, so on an annual basis the cost goal was met, but the quarterly cash figure was materially below the body of the report's claim.

A.4 RISK REGISTER EXTRACT. Risks that MATERIALIZED during the window (from the original January risk register):
  RSK-03 'Credential translation errors' — materialized (incident 2025-06-11).
  RSK-07 'Cache behavior differs from Jenkins' — materialized (incident 2025-06-19).
  RSK-09 'Vendor price increases' — did not materialize; unit prices held.
  RSK-02 'Team resistance' — did not materialize; feedback in Section 5 was positive, with the caveat of the mobile signing complaint, which the meeting classified as a documentation gap rather than resistance.
  RSK-05 'Mobile signing complexity' — the meeting debated whether this materialized; the majority ruled it did NOT materialize as a risk event during the window because signing never failed; it is a scope-completion shortfall instead.

A.5 SIGN-OFF RECORD. The body of the report was peer reviewed by Farid Bergstrom. Final sign-off authority for TR-2025-07 rests with the Head of Platform Engineering; as of 15 July the report carries a conditional sign-off: accepted subject to the addendum corrections being incorporated in a revision.

End of report TR-2025-07.

MAPLE GROVE SECONDARY SCHOOL
PROGRAMME COMMITTEE — MINUTES NO. 41, SPRING TERM
Held Tuesday 11 March, 7:00 p.m., staff room. Drafted by Mrs. E. Whitmore, clerk. A typed-up copy of the clerk's handwritten end-of-evening note is appended at the very end.

1. WELCOME AND ATTENDANCE
The chair opened the meeting at 7:02 p.m. and thanked everyone, most warmly, for giving up their evening. Present: Chiara Nakamura (vice-principal, chairing with great kindness in the principal's absence), Bao Novak (IT coordinator and health & safety lead), Yara Rahman (parent-governor representative), Mr. P. Dunmore (bursar), Miss S. Achebe (head of Year 10), Mrs. E. Whitmore (clerk). Apologies, received with sincere regret, were noted from the principal (county trust conference), the head of catering (unwell, we wish her a speedy recovery), and the caretaker (double-shifted, with the committee's full understanding).

2. MINUTES OF THE LAST MEETING (NO. 40)
The minutes of 5 February were approved as a true record, proposed by Miss Achebe, seconded by Mr. Dunmore, and signed by the chair, who thanked the clerk for such careful work. One tiny correction was politely requested: the fire-drill time should read 11:04 a.m., not 11:40 a.m.

3. MATTERS ARISING
3.1 Fire drill. Mr. Bao Novak reported that the February drill had been completed in 4 minutes 50 seconds, a full 30 seconds slower than October, though still inside the 5-minute target. He thanked everyone for moving so briskly despite the rain.
3.2 Lost keys. Two sets of laboratory keys were misplaced in February and found, thankfully, in the lost-property box. The caretaker has ordered key safes.
3.3 Notice board. The entrance notice board was repainted over half-term; Miss Achebe kindly supplied new pins.

4. TREASURER'S REPORT
Mr. Dunmore presented the accounts with his usual patience. Unrestricted fund balance as at 28 February: €12,447.10, against a forecast of €12,747.10. He drew attention, very gently, to the difference of exactly €300.00, which corresponds to the deposit paid to Tidewater Supply for the stage lighting hire and not yet returned. He has written three extremely courteous letters. A second near-miss figure was explained: the petty-cash float shows €141.20 because a €40.00 taxi receipt is still outstanding. The committee thanked Mr. Dunmore warmly and approved the report unanimously.

5. CATERING
The head of catering sent apologies and a note. Hot-meal uptake rose from 62% to 71% after the new pasta bar. Vegetarian options are now labelled. A request for a second water fountain was noted for the premises sub-committee. The chair thanked the kitchen staff, in absentia, most sincerely.

6. UNIFORM SUPPLIER
The supplier has agreed to stock the lighter summer jumper from April. A parent wrote asking about a fleece; the supplier does not offer one. The committee agreed to reply politely declining. Mr. Dunmore noted that the uniform grant (€95 per eligible student) is separate from fee remission and must never be confused with it — he asks colleagues to read Section 9 before answering parents.

7. TRANSPORT
Quotes for next year's coach work were compared. Tidewater Freight offered €1,980.00 for the snow-sports trip and €640.00 for the summer theatre trip; an alternative firm offered €2,150.00 but for a route that includes an extra pick-up point, so the figures are not directly comparable, and the committee was careful to say so. Mr. Bao Novak reminded everyone that any coach journey over three hours requires a second driver under the transport policy, an exception-free rule that has stood for years.

8. EXAMINATION TIMETABLE
The summer examination week was PUBLISHED ON THE PORTAL AND IN THE FOYER on 1 March as 13–17 May inclusive. Chiara Nakamura asked, with her characteristic courtesy, that no trips, fixtures or rehearsals be scheduled in that week, and that colleagues check the published dates before planning anything, as the week is now fixed and cannot be moved.

9. FEE REMISSION POLICY (READ OUT IN FULL, AS REQUESTED)
The chair read the policy aloud so that the whole committee hears the same words:
"9.1 Families whose confirmed household income for the last complete tax year falls below €38,000 per annum may apply in writing to the bursar for remission of tuition fees.
9.2 Where the bursar is satisfied as to the income figures, remission of the full tuition fee shall be granted for the student named in the application.
9.3 PROVIDED ALWAYS that no student enrolled in the International Baccalaureate stream, including the pre-IB Diploma preparation year, shall be eligible for remission under this policy, in any amount, whatever the household income, as the IB levy funds a separate staffing arrangement that the school cannot lawfully waive.9.4 This policy does not affect the uniform grant, free school meals, or the music-instrument fund, which have their own rules."
The chair noted that Section 9.3 is the exception colleagues most often forget, and she apologised for reading it so slowly.

10. TRIPS AND VISITS APPROVAL POLICY (ALSO READ OUT IN FULL)
"10.1 Day visits: approval by any senior teacher.
10.2 Visits of one overnight stay: approval by the vice-principal.
10.3 Visits of two or more overnight stays: approval by the full programme committee at a quorate meeting.
10.4 PROVIDED ALWAYS that no visit falling wholly or partly within a published examination week shall be approved by any officer, teacher or committee of the school, under any circumstances whatsoever; such applications must be withdrawn and resubmitted for a different week."
Miss Achebe thanked the chair for reading the whole text and said it was very clear.

11. ICT AND PORTAL
Bao Novak reported that the portal was offline for 20 minutes on 27 February for a patch supplied by Kestrel Software, who were, he said, extremely helpful. Password resets now average two hours. A printer in the humanities corridor still jams; a replacement is ordered.

12. ANY OTHER BUSINESS
12.1 Proposed snow-sports visit. Miss Achebe proposed a two-night snow-sports visit for Year 10, departing 14 May and returning 16 May, travelling by coach with Tidewater Freight. She apologised for bringing it so late and said the students were terribly excited. The chair thanked her for her enthusiasm, observed that the dates sit inside the published examination week of 13–17 May, and asked the clerk to record that the matter was discussed. After polite discussion the committee asked Miss Achebe to look at the February half-term instead; she agreed most graciously to reconsider, saying that if the dates must change, they must, and she would rather the students sat their papers properly. She asked, only for completeness, who would have been the proper approving body had the dates been free; the chair referred her to Section 10 as read out.
12.2 Fee remission application from a parent-governor. Yara Rahman declared an interest, apologised for the intrusion, and mentioned that she had submitted a remission application for her daughter Amira, who is in the pre-IB Diploma preparation year. The bursar confirmed the household income on file is €36,200 for the last complete tax year, verified against the tax assessment. The chair thanked Mrs. Rahman for her transparency and asked the clerk to note that Section 9.3 applies to pre-IB preparation year students in the same way as to the Diploma years, as the words "including the pre-IB Diploma preparation year" appear expressly in the policy. The chair apologised twice for having to say so.
12.3 Thank-you cards. The committee agreed, with enormous gratitude, to send cards to the kitchen staff and to the caretaker.

13. DATE OF NEXT MEETING
Tuesday 6 May, 7:00 p.m. The chair thanked everyone again, twice, and closed the meeting at 9:11 p.m.

APPENDIX — clerk's handwritten note, typed up the next morning
"Sat by the door so I could hear everything. Chair was lovely as always. Jobs I was given at the end — Hall for the summer concert: BOOKED, confirmations all signed, thank goodness. — Projector for the hall: still NOT working, Bao promises a spare unit by Friday, so that one is not finished, do not tick it. — Consent letter templates for Year 10 visits: EMAILED to all Year 10 parents tonight, done. — Coach invoice from Tidewater Supply for the theatre trip: PAID in full this afternoon, receipt filed. — Refreshments rota for the concert interval: FILLED, every slot has a name, lovely. — First-aid kit for the minibus: ordered but NOT arrived yet, Bao checks on it tomorrow. — Also: Mrs. Rahman's fee form went to the bursar; I only file these, I do not decide them. Must remember pins for Miss Achebe."

Access was revoked on September 19. Farid noted, with the weariness of a man who has explained this before, that badges do not deactivate themselves out of politeness, and that department heads need to actually submit the offboarding form. Greta asked whether the form could be shorter. Farid said the form is one field long and the field is the person's name. Greta said she would think about it.

3.2 Parental Leave Policy Revision — Status
The draft revision to the parental leave policy, circulated in August, has completed its comment period. Nineteen comments were received. Seventeen were supportive. One asked whether the policy could be extended to pets (it cannot). One asked whether "parental" included "becoming a parent to a boat" (it does not, and Harbor Studio regrets that this required a written response). The revised policy, reproduced in full as Appendix A to these minutes, extends paid parental leave from twelve weeks to sixteen weeks, effective for any leave beginning on or after January 1 of next year. The committee voted: five in favor, zero opposed, zero abstentions, one imaginary vote cast on behalf of the radiator. The motion carried. The finalized policy will be distributed company-wide by Nadia, who also volunteered — this time genuinely, and everyone could tell because she didn't sigh — to rewrite the parental leave FAQ so that it answers questions people actually ask, rather than questions the legal team wishes people would ask. Draft due October 14.

3.3 Remote Work Stipend
Bao confirmed that the monthly remote work stipend — sixty dollars per month for eligible home-based staff — has now been processed correctly for two consecutive pay cycles, which by Harbor Studio standards constitutes a streak. He reminded the committee that the stipend is prospective only: it was never paid retroactively for the months before its adoption, and staff who ask about back payment should be pointed, gently, to the FAQ. Greta asked whether the FAQ could be shorter. See 3.2 for how these conversations generally resolve.

4. NEW BUSINESS

4.1 Four-Day Work Week Proposal
Mateo presented the proposal to shorten the standard work week to four days. He summarized the pilot design: a thirteen-week trial in the design department only, beginning in Q4, with the department's client-facing hours unchanged (design staff would compress their hours into four longer days rather than reduce total hours). Mateo's presentation was eleven slides, of which at least six were charts proving that other companies had tried this and survived, which is a low bar that several companies have nonetheless failed.
Greta expressed support in principle and skepticism in practice, noting that "in principle" is where Harbor Studio keeps most of its best ideas. The committee discussed whether to commit to a permanent company-wide switch. Mateo argued the pilot data should come first. Nadia argued the same thing but louder. Bao asked what happens to payroll calculations if the pilot succeeds, was told "we'll figure it out," and wrote something down that looked suspiciously like a resignation letter outline.
DECISION: The Q4 pilot in the design department was approved, five votes to zero, with the committee directing that no permanent company-wide change be adopted now. A formal review of pilot results is scheduled for the January meeting, and the committee expressly declined to decide anything today about making the shorter week permanent across the company. In other words: the four-day week remains a rumor with a budget line, not a promise.

4.2 Q4 Budget Requests
The committee reviewed the three budget requests submitted for the fourth quarter. The review was brisk, bloodless, and punctuated by Bao's spreadsheet, which he described as "the only honest document in this room."
(a) HR Operations — onboarding software renewal. Requested $12,400 for the annual license of the onboarding platform (the one that makes new hires watch eleven videos about company values before their laptop works). No reduction was proposed. APPROVED IN FULL at $12,400, five votes to zero. This request survived review untouched.
(b) Design Department — conference travel. Requested $8,500 for three staff to attend the Coastal Design Summit. The committee approved the request only after cutting it by twenty percent, to $6,800, on the motion of Greta, who observed that the Summit's primary educational value has historically been the hotel breakfast. APPROVED WITH REDUCTION.
(c) Facilities — wellness room refresh. Requested $3,000 for new chairs and a plants budget for the second-floor wellness room. Quentin's email (see 1, above) defended the plants at length. The committee nonetheless deferred this request to the January meeting pending the Q4 pilot results, on the grounds that the wellness room's current chairs are "ergonomic in the sense that they cause feelings." DEFERRED, NOT FUNDED.
Summary: of the three requests, exactly one was approved exactly as submitted, one was approved at a lower amount, and one was postponed. The spreadsheet, as always, keeps score better than the minutes do.

4.3 Interviewer Training
Nadia raised the ongoing problem of inconsistent interview practices across departments. She proposed a mandatory half-day session on fair and consistent interviewing for everyone who sits on a hiring panel. The committee approved the concept. Nadia will schedule the sessions and enroll the panel members herself; she will also update the standard job posting template so that every posting uses the same structure, salary band disclosure, and — her words — "fewer instances of the phrase 'rockstar' unless we are literally hiring a rockstar." Both items are hers to deliver; the training sessions to be booked by November 8, and the revised posting template due alongside the January meeting.

4.4 Q4 Headcount Forecast
Greta requested a staffing projection for the next quarter — expected new requisitions, planned departures, and internal transfers — to present to the executive team. This deliverable was assigned to Nadia as well, owing to her possession of the recruiting pipeline data, the attrition tracker, and, in Greta's words, "the only functioning crystal ball in this company." Due October 30. Nadia accepted this without visible joy but also without visible despair, which is the standard emotional range for action items in this committee.

4.5 Offboarding Form, Revisited
Farid raised again (see 3.1) that the offboarding form is not the problem; the problem is that nobody files it. The committee agreed to add a reminder to the manager departure checklist. No one was assigned to update the checklist. The checklist will therefore not be updated, and this item will appear in these minutes again in December, as it did in June, wearing a slightly different hat.

5. POLICY REVIEW: OVERTIME AND COMP TIME (Appendix B)
The committee reviewed the overtime provisions of the employee handbook for consistency with the payroll system's recent behavior. The relevant text, reproduced in Appendix B, states: overtime is paid at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours worked beyond forty in a single work week; comp time may be offered only in departments that have opted in via written agreement; comp time never accrues automatically. Bao reported that the payroll system had, for one glorious week in July, automatically granted comp time to the whole accounting department, an act of generosity the system was not authorized to perform. Affected employees received a correction memo. The committee confirmed the handbook text stands as written and needs no amendment; the bug was in the software, not the policy, which is the correct order of things.

6. RADIATOR UPDATE
No formal update was given, but the radiator made a sound at 11:40 a.m. that Mateo described as "a callback to an earlier motif." No action was taken.

7. ACTION ITEM REGISTER
(A) Nadia Haddad — rewrite the parental leave FAQ in plain language. Due October 14.
(B) Nadia Haddad — book and enroll staff in the interviewer fairness sessions. Sessions to be on calendars by November 8.
(C) Nadia Haddad — revise the standard job posting template. Due at the January meeting.
(D) Nadia Haddad — compile the next-quarter staffing projection for the executive team. Due October 30.
(E) Farid Mensah — circulate the completed badge access audit summary to department heads. Due October 4. (Complete audit; summary pending, because a summary requires words.)
(F) Mateo O'Neill — design and launch the Q4 four-day week pilot in the design department. Pilot to begin first week of Q4.
(G) Greta Rahman — distribute the finalized parental leave policy (Appendix A) company-wide. Due October 7.
(H) Quentin Mensah — resubmit the wellness room request in January with, per Greta, "fewer adjectives." Due January meeting.
(I) Nobody — update the manager departure checklist. See 4.5. See also: the void.

8. DATE OF NEXT MEETING
Thursday, January 16, Conference Room B, radiator willing. Greta reminded everyone that attendance is mandatory unless one is actively fighting water at a client site, a standard which Quentin has now, technically, set.

Minutes respectfully submitted by Nadia Haddad, who would like it noted that taking minutes while also owning four action items is a unique form of self-expression.

APPENDIX A — REVISED PARENTAL LEAVE POLICY (FINAL TEXT)
Section 1. Eligibility. All regular full-time employees of Harbor Studio are eligible for paid parental leave following the birth or adoption of a child, or the placement of a child in their care, regardless of gender or caregiving role.
Section 2. Duration. Eligible employees are entitled to sixteen (16) weeks of paid parental leave. This supersedes the prior entitlement of twelve (12) weeks.
Section 3. Effective date. The extended entitlement applies to any leave commencing on or after January 1. Leaves commenced before that date follow the previous twelve-week entitlement for their full duration. There is no retroactive adjustment of leaves already concluded.
Section 4. Notice. Employees should provide at least thirty days' written notice where the leave date is foreseeable.
Section 5. Job protection. The employee's position, or an equivalent one, is held for the duration of the leave.
Section 6. Boats. This policy does not cover vessels of any kind.

APPENDIX B — OVERTIME AND COMP TIME (HANDBOOK TEXT, UNCHANGED)
Section 4.1. Overtime. Hours worked in excess of forty (40) in a single work week are compensated at one and one-half (1.5) times the employee's regular hourly rate.
Section 4.2. Compensatory time. Comp time may be offered only in departments that have executed a written opt-in agreement, and only when requested and approved in advance for a specific occasion. Comp time does not accrue automatically under any circumstances.
Section 4.3. Precedence. Where this section conflicts with any informal practice, custom, or act of the payroll software's initiative, this section controls.

APPENDIX C — QUENTIN MENSAH'S EMAIL, RECEIVED 6:04 A.M., REPRODUCED FOR COMPLETENESS

I apologize for the late notice of my absence and the even later hour of this email. I will submit the wellness room justification in writing; I ask only that the committee consider that the current chairs were purchased when the building was a different company with different spines. Apologies again. — Q. Mensah, Facilities"

RIDGELINE MOTORS OF CALDER VALLEY
NEW ASSOCIATE ONBOARDING CHECKLIST AND REFERENCE MANUAL

Prepared by: Ines Lindqvist, Human Resources Coordinator
Reviewed and approved by: Zoltan Sorensen, General Manager
Issued to: Aiden Bergstrom, Sales Associate (full-time, new hire)
Effective date: Monday, 14 April
Document control: Onboarding Manual, Revision 12. All associates acknowledge receipt of the current revision on their first day; superseded revisions must be returned to Human Resources for shredding. If any statement in this manual appears to conflict with a directive from the General Manager, the directive governs, and the discrepancy should be reported to Ines Lindqvist the same week so the manual can be corrected.

SECTION 1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This manual exists to make your first ninety days at Ridgeline Motors orderly, consistent, and free of guesswork. It consolidates the onboarding checklist, the product knowledge syllabus, the desk procedures for keys and inventory, the working rules of the sales floor, the finance and insurance (F&I) basics every associate must understand before quoting money, the service lane orientation, and the compliance obligations that attach to every customer transaction at a licensed dealership in this state. It is deliberately long. Zoltan Sorensen has directed that no associate should have to rely on hallway folklore to learn how this store operates; folklore, he notes, is what stores rely on when their manuals are out of date, and our manuals are not out of date. Read the whole document once during your first week. During weeks two through thirteen, return to individual sections as your trainer assigns them. Bring your questions to Mateo Mensah, Sales Manager, who owns the training calendar, or to Ines Lindqvist for anything touching payroll, benefits, or personnel records.

The scope of this manual is the sales department. Technicians, detailers, and parts counter staff follow separate manuals maintained by their own supervisors, although Section 9 of this document provides a service lane orientation for sales associates, because customers will ask you service questions in the showroom whether or not you are qualified to answer them, and it is better for everyone that you know which questions to route to Esi Sorensen, our lead service advisor, rather than guessing.

SECTION 2. WHAT THIS STORE SELLS, AND TO WHOM

Ridgeline Motors is a full-line new and pre-owned dealership. Our new-vehicle franchise covers the Ridgeline brand: sedans, crossovers, sport utility vehicles, and a working line of half-ton and three-quarter-ton pickups, plus the electric model introduced two model years ago. Our pre-owned inventory runs from late-model lease returns to trade-ins of every age. Our customer base is the Calder Valley trade area: farms, contractors, two school districts, the hospital, and the professional households of the river towns. Roughly two-thirds of our volume is repeat or referral business. That statistic is repeated at every Monday meeting because it explains most of the rules in this manual: our business depends on people coming back, and people come back when the process is clean, honest, and boring in the best sense of the word. Nothing in this manual is designed to make a sale today at the cost of a customer tomorrow.

SECTION 3. DAY ONE CHECKLIST

Your first day is administrative and orientation only. You will not sell a car on your first day, and you should not try. Report to the HR office on the second floor at 8:30 a.m. Ines Lindqvist will walk you through the following items in order, initialing each line as it is completed. Keep your copy; several later items reference it.

3.1 Identity and eligibility verification. Present original documents establishing identity and work authorization. Photocopies cannot be accepted, and photographs on a phone cannot be accepted, no matter how clear.

3.2 Personnel file. Emergency contact, tax withholding forms, and direct deposit details. Direct deposit takes one to two pay cycles to activate; your first check, if paper, will be handed to you by Ines rather than mailed, so that nothing is lost to a wrong address.

3.3 Offer letter and pay plan. Your offer letter states your base draw, your commission schedule, and the spiff programs currently in effect. The commission schedule is summarized in Appendix C. Sign only the copy Ines provides; drafts circulated by anyone else have no standing.

3.4 Handbook acknowledgment. The general employee handbook covers conduct, attendance, and grievance procedures. This onboarding manual covers the sales floor. You sign for both, separately, because they are separate documents.

3.5 Systems access. Your user account for the dealership management system (DMS), the customer relationship manager (CRM), and the inventory pricing tool will be created on day one. Temporary passwords expire after the first login; if your account locks, call the help desk, do not ask a colleague to log in for you, and never work under another associate's login. Every deal you touch must be traceable to you.

3.6 Keys, badge, and locker. You will be issued an associate badge, which opens the staff entrance after hours, and a locker in the sales bullpen. The badge is property of the store; report a lost badge to Ines the same day. There is a replacement charge only if the badge is lost twice in one year.

3.7 Safety orientation. Fire exits, extinguisher locations, the spill kit in the detail bay, and the severe weather muster point at the interior wall of the service reception. This item takes twenty minutes and Ines will not rush it.

3.8 Lunch with Zoltan Sorensen. The General Manager takes every new associate to lunch on day one. It is not an interview and nothing you say over lunch goes in your file. Its purpose is simple: he wants every associate to be able to recognize him in the lot, and he wants to hear, in your words, why you took the job.

SECTION 4. WEEK ONE: THE FLOOR, THE DESK, AND THE KEYS

Week one is spent shadowing. You will be assigned to a senior associate each morning by Mateo Mensah and you will follow one customer interaction per day from greeting to close, or from greeting to a scheduled return, which is often the better outcome. In the afternoons you return to the classroom modules in Section 5. By Friday of week one you should be able to do the following without prompting: greet a walk-in within the standard described below, pull up a unit in the DMS, locate its key, walk the customer to the unit, and describe its equipment honestly — which sometimes means saying "I don't know; let me check," a sentence that costs nothing and is always available to you.

4.1 The greeting standard. Every customer entering the showroom or the lot is greeted within thirty seconds of arrival, by name if known, by eye contact and a hello if not. The greeting is a greeting. It is not an interrogation. Ask what brought them in; do not ask how they will be paying. Customers who want to browse alone should be told, truthfully, that you will be at the desk if anything comes up, and then you must actually be at the desk where you said you would be.

4.2 Key control. This is the rule the General Manager checks personally, so read this paragraph twice. All keys stay with the desk at all times. There are no exceptions for favorites, for units you are personally selling, for the EV demonstrator, or for the truck you think someone is about to come back for. Keys hang on the control board behind the sales desk, each on a numbered tag matching the stock number of the unit. To take a key, you sign it out on the clipboard with the stock number, your initials, and the time; you sign it back in the same way. Keys go back on the board the moment a customer leaves, not at the end of your shift, and never in a pocket, never in a drawer, and never taken home. If a customer is handed a key for a test drive, the associate conducting the drive holds the key for the entire drive; it does not go to the customer's pocket even for the leg of the drive the customer drives. Losing a key for a unit on the floor is a writeable incident because it strands a saleable vehicle behind the glass with no way to start it. Pre-owned units in the back lot keep their keys in the lockbox cabinet; the cabinet is emptied into the board each morning by the opening manager and returned at close.

4.3 The lot walk. Each morning at 8:50, the floor team walks the entire lot, front and back, before the doors open at 9:00. The walk checks four things: every unit is locked; every window sticker is present and legible; every unit is parked within its lined space with no overhang into the drive lanes; and any unit with body damage, flat tires, or missing equipment is flagged with a red card on the windshield and logged in the damage book at the desk. The lot walk takes fifteen minutes when done properly and forty minutes when done after the first customer arrives, which is why it is done before.

4.4 Showroom conduct. Coffee station restocked before open. Demo units inside polished, windows clean, trunks closed, and placards straight. Personal calls on the floor are taken outside or at the bullpen, not in the showroom, and never while a customer is within sight of you. The showroom telephone is answered by whoever is nearest when it rings, on the second ring at the latest, with "Ridgeline Motors, this is" and your first name.

SECTION 5. PRODUCT KNOWLEDGE SYLLABUS

You cannot sell what you cannot describe, and you will be tested. Module tests are administered by Mateo Mensah at the end of weeks one, three, and six. A score of eighty percent is passing; a lower score means you retake the module after a review session, and there is no penalty for a retake other than the time it takes.

Module 1 (week 1): The sedan line. Engines, trim ladder, standard versus optional equipment, and the three most common misconceptions customers arrive with, which are, in order of frequency: that the base trim has heated seats (it does not), that the hybrid sedan requires a plug (it does not; it self-charges), and that the top trim is required to get the safety package (it is not; the safety package is optional on every trim).

Module 2 (week 3): Crossovers and SUVs. Seating configurations, towing differences between the two- and three-row models, cargo measurements, and the family buyer's questions, which are almost always about the second row: does it fold flat, does it recline, does a rear-facing infant seat fit behind a six-foot driver. You will be expected to demonstrate the second-row fold in under thirty seconds and to install a display infant seat correctly. If you have never installed one, say so in training; this is exactly what training is for.

Module 3 (week 3): Pickups. Payload versus towing, the trailer brake controller, bed lengths, and the trade customer's calendar. Contractors buy on schedules, not on mood; the associate who understands that a crew cab with a short bed is a different tool than a regular cab with a long bed will earn the contractor's repeat business for a decade.

Module 4 (week 6): The electric model and the Level 2 charger program. Range figures and what they do and do not promise, home charging assessment, the federal and state incentive paperwork we assist with at the F&I desk, and the cold-weather range conversation, which must be honest. On the EV, honesty is a compliance matter as much as a sales matter: range claims in our advertising are manufacturer figures, and our obligation is to present them as manufacturer figures, not as promises made by this store.

Module 5 (week 6): Pre-owned certification. Which pre-owned units qualify for the certified program, the inspection the certification requires, the warranty terms, and, critically, what certification does not include. A certified unit is not a new unit. Its warranty is the certified program's warranty, and its coverage periods are printed in the buyer's guide on the window. Know where to point on the buyer's guide; never paraphrase warranty terms from memory during a sale.

SECTION 6. TRADE-INS AND APPRAISALS

The trade-in is where more customer trust is won or lost than anywhere else in the deal, because it is where the customer's emotions are highest and where the numbers are least understood. Ridgeline Motors appraises every trade honestly, in writing, whether or not the customer buys from us.

6.1 The intake. The customer's unit is walked with the customer present. You record mileage, equipment, tires, glass, body condition, interior condition, and service history the customer can recall. You do not appraise. Appraisal is performed by Mateo Mensah or by the pre-owned buyer using the store's subscription pricing tools, the auction terminal, and their own eyes on the unit. Your job on intake is to document accurately, because the written appraisal is only as good as the intake sheet behind it.

6.2 The written appraisal. Every appraisal is written, on the appraisal form, showing comparable market values and the adjustment for condition and reconditioning cost. The appraisal is presented to the customer by the associate with the manager available for questions. The customer keeps a copy whether they buy or not.

6.3 Negative equity. When a trade-in is worth less than the payoff owed on it, the difference between the appraised value and the payoff is negative equity. This is common, it is not a reflection on the customer, and it must never be described as though it were. Under our standard practice the difference is added to the amount financed at signing, so the customer finances the shortfall together with the new vehicle's balance rather than paying it out of pocket at the desk. The F&I manager, Wanjiru Kaur, will present the exact numbers. Associates do not improvise payment quotes on negative equity deals; the arithmetic belongs to the desk, because a wrong payment quote spoken in the showroom is a promise this store will be asked to keep.

6.4 Payoff quotes. A payoff quote is lender-specific and has an expiration date, usually ten days. A payoff quote older than its good-through date is not a payoff figure; it is a memory of one. Reconfirm payoffs older than their good-through date with the lender before drawing final paperwork, without exception, even when the customer insists the number has not changed, because the customer is sometimes wrong in a direction that costs them money.

SECTION 7. DEMONSTRATIONS AND ROAD TESTS

7.1 Licensing. No road test leaves the lot unless the customer presents a valid driver's license and the associate records the license number on the road test form. No license, no drive; a learner's permit without a licensed adult passenger is not a valid license for this purpose. This rule has no exception for the customer's spouse, for the customer who "always drives with an expired one and it's fine," or for anyone in a hurry.

7.2 Route. The standard road test route is posted at the desk: out the north exit, two laps of the park loop, and the merge onto Route 9 and back. The route takes twenty minutes and includes a hill, a rough patch of pavement for suspension feel, and a merge. Customers who ask to drive farther may, within reason and with the associate's judgment, but every road test returns to the lot before any paperwork is discussed. Driving a customer's trade as part of the appraisal follows the same route.

7.3 Insurance. The customer's own policy covers them on our plates under the standard garage endorsement for demonstration purposes; associates are additionally covered under the store's policy while riding along. If a customer states their license is suspended or revoked, do not proceed with any road test, and note the conversation in the CRM.

7.4 Accidents on road tests. Stop, check for injuries, call emergency services if anyone is hurt or if any other vehicle is involved, exchange information, and call the dealership immediately. Do not admit fault, do not discuss fault with anyone at the scene, and do not continue the demonstration after any collision, however minor. The sales manager comes to the scene. This is a rule about you as much as about the store: associates have been injured standing on the shoulder of Route 9 deciding to "just head back." Do not.

SECTION 8. WORKING THE F&I DESK

Wanjiru Kaur, Finance and Insurance Manager, owns every number that becomes a payment. Week five of your onboarding includes two full days sitting at the F&I desk as an observer. The purpose is not to train you to quote money — you will not — but so that you understand what happens to your deal after the customer says yes, and can therefore describe the process honestly and calmly to a nervous buyer.

8.1 What you may quote. You may discuss prices as marked, current advertised offers with their expiration dates, and the general structure of the process. You may not quote payments, APRs, term options, or monthly figures of any kind. The sentence to memorize is: "The exact numbers are prepared by our finance manager, and here is how that works." Every associate, however senior, defers payments to the desk. This is not a limitation on you; it is the store's promise to the customer that every payment figure they hear is prepared on the same calculator by the same accountable person.

8.2 Products presented at the desk. The F&I desk presents, where applicable and lawful: retail installment terms through our lending partners, the manufacturer's finance offers, service contracts, guaranteed asset protection (GAP) coverage on financed deals, and tire and wheel protection. Every product is presented with its price and its contract terms in writing; no product is described as "required" unless it is required by law or by the lender's condition, and the state regulator's wording on this point is in the compliance binder, which any customer may ask to see and which must be produced on request.

8.3 Spot delivery. When a customer signs the retail contract and takes the vehicle home the same day while the lender's final approval is still pending, the transaction is a spot delivery. Spot deliveries are lawful, common, and disclosed: the buyer's order states that the sale is contingent on assignment of the retail contract to a lender on the terms disclosed, and that if final terms cannot be assigned on the disclosed terms, the store will offer the customer terms as close as practicable or unwind the transaction and return the trade and down payment. Understand the definition before you observe the desk, because customers will ask you what "contingent" means while sitting in the F&I waiting area, and the honest one-sentence answer is that final approval can still take a day or two after the customer signs, which is why the paperwork says what it says. If a spot delivery cannot be assigned on the disclosed terms, Wanjiru calls the customer — the associate who sold the unit is welcome to join the call and often should, but the terms conversation belongs to the desk.

8.4 Money handling. Associates do not take cash deposits, do not hold checks, and do not accept payment cards on the floor. All money moves through the F&I office with a written receipt given at the moment of receipt. A customer who insists on handing you a deposit at the showroom table is walked to the F&I office, pleasantly, every time.

SECTION 9. THE SERVICE LANE ORIENTATION

Week four includes a half-day orientation with Esi Sorensen, lead service advisor. The purpose, again, is triage rather than expertise. You should come away able to do four things: book a service appointment at the advisor's counter; explain the difference between the express maintenance lane and a scheduled repair; hand a customer to Esi or her team by name; and recognize the three questions that must always go to the service department rather than being answered from the sales floor: anything about warranty coverage of a specific failure, anything about a repair charge estimate, and anything about a recall notice the customer received in the mail. You may confirm that a recall notice exists in the system; you may not characterize its scope or severity. Recall work is performed by the service department on the manufacturer's terms, and the associate who "helps" by paraphrasing a recall letter on the showroom floor is creating a commitment the service department did not make.

The service lane also matters to you commercially. Every oil change customer in the express lane is a future buyer of something. The associates who do best at this store long-term are the ones the service lane trusts, and the service lane trusts associates who tell customers the truth about what the service department does and does not do. Esi's standing offer to every new associate is a seat at her counter any morning it is slow, and her standing warning is that it is never slow on Saturdays.

SECTION 10. CUSTOMER FOLLOW-UP AND CRM

The CRM is the store's institutional memory. If it is not in the CRM, it did not happen, and if it is in the CRM, it belongs to the store, which is why the manual is explicit about what gets recorded.

10.1 Recording. Every customer contact is logged the day it occurs: walk-ins, calls, texts with the customer's consent noted, e-mails, road tests, appraisals, and no-shows for scheduled appointments. Log the substance in two sentences. Logs are read by your colleagues covering your days off, and the test of a good log entry is whether your colleague can serve the customer tomorrow from your entry alone.

10.2 Follow-up after a sale. The delivery of a vehicle is the beginning of the follow-up calendar, not the end of the deal. Within two business days of delivery, the selling associate must complete the following actions and log each one in the CRM under the delivery record: place and log the thank-you call to the customer, confirming that the vehicle is performing as expected and that the customer knows who to call if anything is not; confirm that the customer has registered on the owner's portal and, if not, walk them through registration while you have them on the phone; schedule the first service reminder in the CRM so that the system generates the maintenance reminder for the customer's first service interval; and send the post-delivery satisfaction survey link. The survey link goes out in the same two-business-day window, not later, because response rates fall sharply once the newness of the vehicle wears off. Later actions sit on their own schedule: the thirty-day check-in call, the sixty-day courtesy contact, and the annual needs review, each generated by the CRM and each requiring the associate to record an outcome, including the outcome "customer asked not to be contacted," which must be honored immediately and logged verbatim.

10.3 Unsold customers. A customer who leaves without purchasing is logged with the reason, the units of interest, and the agreed next contact date. The next contact is made on the date agreed, not earlier, because "I said Friday and he called Wednesday" is the single most common complaint in any follow-up file, and it is entirely preventable.

10.4 Do-not-contact. Any customer request to stop contact is honored across all channels within one business day of the request, and the flag is never removed without written direction from Zoltan Sorensen. This rule has no exception for a customer who "only meant the texts."

SECTION 11. COMPLIANCE BASICS FOR THE SALES FLOOR

Compliance at a dealership is not a department; it is a set of habits on the floor. The habits you must build in your first ninety days are these.

11.1 Truth in advertising. Advertised prices include all dealer-added equipment already on the unit and disclose rebates that require specific qualifications. When a customer asks about an advertised price, produce the advertisement and read it together rather than paraphrasing it. If the customer does not qualify for a qualification-based rebate, say which qualification they do not meet, and let Wanjiru's desk do the rest.

11.2 Buyer's guide on used units. Every pre-owned unit displays the federal buyer's guide stating whether it is sold as-is or with a warranty, and what the warranty covers. The buyer's guide that is on the window at the time of sale is the buyer's guide that goes into the deal jacket. If the window card is missing or defaced at the time of sale, stop the deal and get a replacement printed; do not proceed and fix it later, because there is no later for a disclosure that was never made.

11.3 Licensing and titling. Title applications, lien recording, and temporary plates are handled by the title clerk. Associates never tell a customer that a title will "take about a week" unless the title clerk has said so for that transaction; the honest answer is "our title clerk handles this and will call you with the exact date," followed by making sure the title clerk actually calls.

11.4 Equal treatment. Every customer receives the same process, the same product presentations, the same pricing transparency, and the same follow-up, without regard to any protected characteristic, and without regard to any assumption about who is the decision-maker in a couple or a group. Ask who will be the registered owner; never assume it from who spoke first.

11.5 Prompt reporting. Suspected odometer discrepancies, flood-damaged trade-ins presented as clean, or any customer statement suggesting title fraud go to Zoltan Sorensen the same day, in writing, even if you are not sure. Uncertainty is a reason to report; it is not a reason to wait.

SECTION 12. HOURS, PAY, AND ATTENDANCE

Showroom hours are 9:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Monday through Saturday, closed Sunday. Sales floor schedules are published two weeks ahead by Mateo Mensah. Weekend coverage is a condition of the sales role; the standard floor week includes every other Saturday. Your pay plan is summarized in Appendix C and consists of a weekly draw against commissions, with commission computed on delivered units per the schedule, and manufacturer spiffs paid when the manufacturer pays them, which can lag a cycle. Attendance: call Mateo by 7:30 a.m. for a same-day absence. Three unlogged absences in ninety days triggers a review under the handbook, not this manual. PTO is requested in the HR system; PTO during the last three days of a month, which is our delivery peak, requires the General Manager's approval, and he grants it more often than people assume, but he cannot grant what he is not asked for.

SECTION 13. FIRST-NINETY-DAY MILESTONES

Day 30: modules 1 and 2 passed; ten logged customer interactions; lot walk certified by the opening manager. Day 60: modules 3 and 4 passed; one supervised deal delivered start to finish; service lane orientation completed. Day 90: all modules passed; two deals delivered with the trainer observing rather than assisting; F&I observation days completed; ninety-day review with Zoltan Sorensen and Mateo Mensah, which is a conversation, not an examination, and which begins with the question the General Manager asks everyone at ninety days: "What in this manual turned out to be wrong?" He asks because it is how the manual gets its next revision, and Revision 13 will be written, in part, from your answer.

APPENDIX A. DOCUMENTARY FEES AND STANDARD CHARGES (CURRENT)
Documentation fee: $225 per retail transaction, itemized on the buyer's order. Title and registration: passed through at cost, itemized. Temporary plate: $12. Dealer-installed accessories: at the marked price on the buyer's order, never bundled silently into the vehicle price. Miscellaneous shop supplies, where incurred on a serviced unit: itemized per the service menu. There is no charge for the first owner's portal registration, the first remote battery replacement, or coffee, ever, and any customer told otherwise should be introduced to Ines Lindqvist personally.

APPENDIX B. NEW MODEL LINEUP SNAPSHOT (TRAINING COPY)
Base sedan, 4 cyl, 8-speed automatic; Hybrid sedan, self-charging, no plug; Premium sedan, turbo 4, optional safety package; Crossover S, 2-row, 5-passenger; Crossover L, 3-row, 7-passenger, optional tow package; Sport utility, body-on-frame, standard tow rating per brochure in deal jacket; Half-ton pickup, three cab styles, two bed lengths; Three-quarter-ton pickup, crew cab only this model year, diesel optional; Electric crossover, single motor standard, dual motor optional, home charger assessment through the F&I desk. Fuel economy figures on this snapshot are the manufacturer's and are quoted from the window sticker, never from this appendix, which is a training copy and expires when the model year does.

APPENDIX C. PAY PLAN SUMMARY (SUMMARY ONLY; THE OFFER LETTER GOVERNS)
Weekly draw against commission, drawn amount recovered from earned commission per the offer letter schedule. Commission schedule per delivered unit: new vehicles per the published grid by model line; pre-owned per the front-end gross grid; certified units carry the certified increment. Manufacturer spiffs are additional and paid on manufacturer timing. No commission is earned on a deal that unwinds, and no associate is penalized for a deal that is walked away from honestly — the store's position, stated by the General Manager at hire, is that a clean lost sale is a future customer and a dirty won one is a former one.

APPENDIX D. FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS FROM NEW ASSOCIATES
"Can I park in the customer lot?" No; the staff lot is behind the pre-owned row.
"What if I know the answer to a payment question?" You still defer to the desk. The rule is about accountability, not ability.
"Can I take a demo home overnight?" Demonstration assignments are made by Zoltan Sorensen in writing only, after ninety days, and never to associates still in draw recovery.
"Who do I call if the alarm goes off when I'm closing?" The list is at the desk; you call the manager on duty first, non-emergency line second, and you stay on the property only if it is safe to do so.
"Do I have to log the rude customer?" You log the facts of the interaction, not your assessment of the person's character, and you take the incident to Mateo if it involved threats, discrimination, or anyone feeling unsafe.
"What does 'contingent' mean on the buyer's order?" It means what Section 8.3 says it means, and Section 8.3 is the answer you give.

APPENDIX E. GLOSSARY (SELECTION)
Buyer's order: the purchase agreement itemizing vehicle, price, trade, and fees. Buyer's guide: the federal window disclosure on pre-owned units. DMS: dealership management system. CRM: customer relationship manager. Draw: advance against earned commission. F&I: finance and insurance. GAP: guaranteed asset protection coverage on financed deals. Payoff: amount owed on an existing loan, valid through its good-through date. Spot delivery: see Section 8.3. Unwind: reversal of a delivered transaction, returning all parties to their prior positions.

End of manual. Acknowledge receipt to Ines Lindqvist. Questions on content to Mateo Mensah; questions on personnel matters to Ines Lindqvist; anything the manual does not cover, to Zoltan Sorensen, whose door is genuinely open, which you may verify on day one at lunch.
