INCIDENT POSTMORTEM — THE FREEZER NIGHT AT THE LARKSPUR GRAND
Prepared by Xiu Haddad, Director of Operations, Larkspur Grand Hotel & Bistro
Written over the course of about two weeks, because honestly every time I sat down to finish this something else exploded, which is kind of the theme of this whole document, so please forgive the rambling. Also please forgive the length. I was told to be thorough and I have taken that instruction to an unhealthy extreme.

1. THE SHORT VERSION

On the night of Friday, October 11th, the walk-in freezer in the main kitchen of the Larkspur Grand failed silently sometime between 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. Nobody noticed until the breakfast prep crew came in at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday, October 12th, and by then the internal temperature had climbed from its normal minus-18 Celsius all the way up to plus-4 Celsius. The compressor had died. We ended up discarding roughly $18,400 worth of food, closing the hotel bistro for Saturday dinner service and Sunday brunch, moving a chunk of our frozen stock into a rented refrigerated trailer that Granite Rentals very kindly dropped off at 7:15 a.m. Saturday, and refunding or comping a total of $3,842 in guest charges across the affected weekend. We got the freezer itself back up and running at 8:40 p.m. Saturday evening, which — given that the technician from Kestrel Supply didn't even get the first parts delivery from Meridian Supply until nearly 2 p.m. — is honestly a small miracle, and I want to say that up front because the rest of this document is going to be a lot of me complaining about processes and I don't want anyone reading it to think the actual humans dropped the ball. The humans were great. The processes were not.

2. HOW IT ALL STARTED, WHICH IS TO SAY, HOW NOBODY NOTICED ANYTHING WAS WRONG

The Larkspur Grand is a 212-room property. That particular weekend we were at 71% occupancy, which for mid-October in this market is honestly fine, not great, not terrible. Friday night we had about 150 guests in house, a wedding block of 44 people from the Odum-Antwi party (lovely family, more on them later because they deserve their own paragraph), and a fairly normal slate of restaurant reservations.

The walk-in freezer in question is the big one, the 20-cubic-meter unit we use for all primary protein storage: the short ribs, the salmon portions, the veal stock, the duck confit that Chef Dalia Sorensen had been curing for the autumn menu launch, all of it. It was installed in 2019, serviced on a contract by Kestrel Supply, and — this is the part that stings — it had passed a preventive maintenance inspection on September 24th, barely two and a half weeks before it died. I want to be fair here: the September inspection was real, it was thorough, the technician noted that the compressor was 'aging but within tolerance,' and there was no recommendation to replace anything. So this is not a story about a skipped inspection. It is a story about the fact that a compressor can be within tolerance on a Tuesday and dead on a Friday, and if you have no monitoring on it, you find out from the smell.

Which brings me to the monitoring question, and I'll just say it plainly because it's the single most important finding of this whole report: we had no automatic temperature monitoring on that freezer. None. The kitchen team logged temperatures manually twice a day, at 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., which is exactly what our food safety plan said to do. And you know what? The 7 p.m. log on Friday, October 11th, read minus-18 Celsius, entered by sous chef Marcus Teller, and that reading was accurate at the time. The failure happened after that reading. The next scheduled reading would have been 7 a.m. Saturday, and even that would have been too late to save the food, but it would have been two and a half hours earlier than when we actually found out, and in an incident like this two and a half hours is the difference between 'we lost some stock' and 'we lost essentially everything.'

We found out, specifically, at 4:32 a.m., when line cook Beatriz Lindqvist opened the freezer door to pull the sausage for the breakfast gravy, and she told me later — and I'm quoting her from our conversation because it made me laugh in a dark way — 'it smelled like a fish market in July in there.' Beatriz did everything right, by the way. She immediately grabbed the infrared thermometer gun, confirmed the interior was reading plus-4, and called the duty manager, Sven Fischer, at 4:35 a.m., who called me at 4:41 a.m. I live eleven minutes from the property. I was in the parking lot by 5:00 a.m. wearing pajama pants under my raincoat, which several members of the breakfast shift have apparently never let me forget.

3. THE TIMELINE, WHICH I HAVE RECONSTRUCTED FROM TEXTS, THE KITCHEN LOG, AND MY OWN FOGGY MEMORY

I'll do this as a proper minute-by-minute because our insurance adjuster asked for it and honestly it forced me to be more honest about the gaps.

4:32 a.m., Sat Oct 12 — Beatriz Lindqvist discovers the failure during breakfast prep.
4:35 a.m. — Beatriz notifies duty manager Sven Fischer.
4:41 a.m. — Sven calls me (Xiu Haddad) and also pulls up the emergency vendor contact sheet.
4:50 a.m. — Sven reaches the 24-hour dispatch line at Kestrel Supply. They commit to sending their on-call refrigeration technician, Kwame Novak, with an ETA of 'by 7 a.m., traffic depending.'
5:05 a.m. — I call Granite Rentals and ask for a refrigerated trailer, any refrigerated trailer, as soon as humanly possible. Their driver shows up at 7:15 a.m., which frankly stunned me, and I've since sent their ops manager a very gushing thank-you email.
5:20 a.m. — Chef Dalia Sorensen arrives (she was not scheduled; she heard from Beatriz and just came in, which tells you everything about her). She and Sven begin the triage: what's still safe, what's borderline, what's dead.
5:30 a.m. to 6:45 a.m. — The triage. This is the part of the morning I keep replaying. Dalia made the call — and I want to state for the record that I fully backed her — that anything above plus-2 interior temp for protein was going to be discarded per our HACCP plan, and since the whole box had drifted to plus-4 and sat there for hours, that meant essentially all of it. She kept maybe 15% of the frozen vegetables and the bread stock, which we moved to the trailer and to the pastry freezer in the banquet kitchen (that unit, a much smaller 6-cubic-meter box, was fine the whole time, for whatever reason; the small units have their own compressor).
7:00 a.m. — Kwame Novak of Kestrel Supply arrives. He confirms within about twenty minutes that the compressor is the problem: the fan runs, the lights run, the compressor does not. He says he'll need a replacement unit and possibly a new start capacitor, and those parts are not on his van.
7:15 a.m. — Granite Rentals trailer arrives. Kwame helps us run the food that was still viable into it. I want to note this because it's technically not his job and he did it anyway.
9:40 a.m. — Kwame confirms the exact part numbers needed and places the order through Meridian Supply, our parts distributor, which opens at 9. He initially hoped a compressor was in stock at their regional depot, forty-five minutes away; it was not, and the one they had was at the further warehouse.
1:52 p.m. — Meridian Supply delivers the replacement compressor and capacitor to the loading dock. This was the long scary stretch, 9:40 to 1:52, where we all just kind of stood around a broken freezer making small talk.
2:10 p.m. — Kwame begins the swap. Dalia decides, in parallel, to cancel Saturday dinner service in the bistro. This was the right call: even if the freezer came back, the food that would go in it wasn't there anymore, and the walk-in cooler (the fridge, the separate unit) was by now stuffed beyond safe capacity with everything we'd rescued.
8:40 p.m. — Freezer back online, holding minus-16 and trending down. Kwame stays until almost 10 p.m. making sure it cycles correctly, refuses my offer of dinner (everything was comped anyway; he took a coffee and a slice of banana bread from the pastry section, which survived).
Sunday, Oct 13 — Bistro still closed for brunch; Dalia and her team work a special limited a-la-carte dinner menu using the small banquet freezer plus same-day deliveries from two suppliers. Chef knocked it out of the park, honestly, but more on the guest reaction later.
Monday, Oct 14 — Full kitchen operations resume. We placed our restocking orders that morning.

4. WHAT WE LOST, IN DOLLARS, BECAUSE THE ACCOUNTING TEAM MADE ME PUT THIS IN

Total food discarded: $18,410 at last inventory value. The big-ticket items: about $6,200 in beef (short ribs, tenderloin ends, a whole striploin), $3,100 in salmon and other seafood, $2,800 in the duck confit and cured items Chef Dalia had been aging since early September, and the rest a mix of poultry, pork, frozen pastry components, and about $700 of ice cream and sorbet for the dessert menu which Beatriz was genuinely mournful about. The $700 figure includes the wedding cake flowers that were being held for the Odum-Antwi cake, although those were actually fine and got moved out in time, so I should say $700 of dessert stock minus the flowers. Let's call the ice cream $640 to be safe. Actually, the inventory sheet says $18,410 total, so I'll trust the sheet.

Guest refunds and comps: $3,842 total for the weekend. This breaks down as follows: the Odum-Antwi wedding block got their Saturday-night dinner moved from the bistro to the ballroom with a complimentary upgrade, and because we comped the wine pairings for the rehearsal-adjacent dinner they'd booked, that was $1,450 of the total; nineteen separate room charges had the resort fee and breakfast package removed, which accounted for $1,187; the rest — $1,205 — was individual bistro reservation cancellations where we comped a future-meal voucher at face value and covered the corkage on a few tables that had already been seated Saturday before we closed. There's a spreadsheet in Appendix C with every line if anyone wants to argue with me about it, and I know at least one person in revenue does.

The trailer rental from Granite Rentals was $680 for the weekend, and the emergency parts and labor from Kestrel Supply came to $4,315 including the after-hours call-out premium. The freezer itself, since people keep asking, is a 2019 unit that was fully depreciated anyway, and the repair means we did NOT have to buy a new one, which is the one piece of genuinely good financial news in this section.

5. WHAT WE DID ABOUT IT, I.E., THE CORRECTIVE ACTIONS, AND I'M GOING TO BE VERY CAREFUL ABOUT TENSES HERE BECAUSE IT MATTERS

Our regional manager, Sven Iyer (yes, we have a Sven Fischer and a Sven Iyer; no, they are not related; yes, the payroll system confuses them constantly and it caused a genuinely funny mix-up during this incident when both Svens were on the same phone call), asked me to separate what we HAVE done from what we INTEND to do, because apparently last time I wrote one of these reports everything was in past tense and it made a bunch of planned stuff look finished, which is exactly the kind of sloppiness this section exists to prevent. So, carefully:

Completed as of the date of this report (October 25th):

First, we replaced the compressor. That's obviously done — the freezer's been running since October 12th and Kestrel Supply came back on the 17th for a follow-up check and signed off on it. The unit is holding minus-18 like a champ.

Second, we installed continuous temperature monitoring. This is the one I'm proudest of. As of October 16th, BOTH the walk-in freezer and the walk-in cooler have wired sensors with a cloud dashboard, and the system sends SMS alerts to the duty manager, the exec chef, and me if either unit drifts more than 3 degrees above setpoint for more than 20 minutes. We tested it deliberately on the 16th by propping the cooler door open, and all three of us got the alert within 22 minutes, so it works. Kwame Novak actually recommended the sensor kit and walked our maintenance guy through the mounting, again not technically his job.

Third, we completed HACCP refresher training for the entire kitchen brigade. Dalia ran two sessions on October 15th and 16th covering the discard decision tree and temperature logging, and every member of the kitchen staff, all twenty-six of them, signed off. The morning-log schedule also changed from twice daily to three times daily: 7 a.m., 3 p.m., and 11 p.m., and the 11 p.m. reading is now a closing-checklist item that two people initial.

Fourth — and this one isn't in the kitchen at all — we rewrote the emergency vendor contact sheet, which turned out to be two years out of date and had Granite Rentals listed under the wrong division. Fixed, laminated, posted in three places.

Planned but NOT completed as of the report date:

We have a proposal, sitting on Sven Iyer's desk as I type this, to add the freezer and cooler circuits to a backup power plan, possibly a portable generator tie-in. Sven Iyer is supportive, the ownership group has not yet approved the spend, so: planned, not done. I keep saying 'we'll get the generator sorted' and I need everyone to understand that's future tense.

We also intend to move our quarterly produce purchasing review to a monthly cadence, and Dalia has floated consolidating dry-goods orders under Meridian Supply to get a better rate, but neither of those has happened; the produce supplier situation is unchanged as of this writing.

And, because someone will ask: we did NOT change our primary refrigeration service vendor. Kestrel Supply stays. They earned it on October 12th.

6. GUEST AND STAFF REACTION, INCLUDING THE PARTS THAT WEREN'T VERY FUN

For the most part the weekend went better socially than it had any right to. The Odum-Antwi wedding was the big worry. Their Saturday-evening reception dinner was booked in the bistro's private room for 44 guests, and moving that on six hours' notice to the ballroom, with banquet staff instead of bistro staff, could have been a disaster. It was not. The ballroom team, who had the space free, treated it like their own wedding, and the mother of the bride told Sven Fischer it was 'somehow even nicer than what we planned, which is a sentence I never expected to say to a hotel.' I nearly cried in the corridor when he relayed that, not that I told him.

Not everything was rosy. A guest in room 714, whose name I won't put in this report but who filled out a comment card in what I can only describe as aggressive cursive, was furious that Sunday brunch was cancelled and felt the voucher we offered was insufficient; his comment card used the phrase 'bait and switch' three times. Guest services followed up with him personally on Tuesday and he accepted a second voucher, so I think that's resolved, but it's in Appendix B for completeness.

We also had some genuinely lovely reactions. A couple from the wedding block posted a public review of the hotel that same weekend, and I'm going to quote a piece of it because Dalia printed it out and taped it inside the kitchen door: 'The restaurant had some kind of equipment emergency and closed, and instead of shrugging, the hotel threw together the best meal of our whole weekend in a different room with waiters who treated us like the only party in the building. The duck, which the chef apparently rescued by hand, was unbelievable. We came for a wedding and left as fans of the hotel itself.' Five stars. We do not deserve it and we're framing it anyway.

Staff-wise, I want to name names in the good column: Beatriz Lindqvist for the discovery and textbook notification chain; Sven Fischer for holding the fort from 4:35 to 5:00 alone; Dalia Sorensen for the triage call and for working, and I counted the hours, a nineteen-hour day; Kwame Novak from Kestrel Supply for the repair and for the extra help beyond scope; and the Granite Rentals driver, whose name I embarrassingly failed to get, who got the trailer to us in under two hours on a Saturday morning. In the 'needs coaching' column: the breakfast shift lead on duty Friday night signed the closing checklist at 10:40 p.m. without doing the freezer listen-check that the checklist requires, which wouldn't have caught a compressor that was fine at 10:40 anyway, but the checklist says it and it wasn't done, so it goes in the report.

7. APPENDICES

Appendix A — Vendor involvement summary. Kestrel Supply: refrigeration service contractor; performed the diagnosis, ordered parts, completed the compressor replacement; total invoice $4,315. Meridian Supply: parts distributor; sourced and delivered the replacement compressor and start capacitor; delivery completed 1:52 p.m. Oct 12; no other role in the incident. Granite Rentals: equipment rental company; provided the emergency refrigerated trailer at 7:15 a.m. Oct 12 and collected it Monday morning; invoice $680. Northwind Labs: I mention them only because our new temperature monitoring dashboard is software built by Northwind Labs, and their onboarding rep was helpful during the October 16th setup, but they were not involved in the incident itself and had no role on October 12th. Northwind Labs also offers a predictive-maintenance module we're evaluating, quote pending, nothing decided.

Appendix B — Complaint log. One formal complaint (room 714 guest, Sunday brunch cancellation, resolved Tuesday Oct 15 with second voucher). Three minor verbal grumbles about brunch, all apologized to at the time. One written compliment from the Odum-Antwi family, and the five-star public review quoted in section 6.

Appendix C — Financial detail. Food loss $18,410 (inventory sheet value). Guest refunds and comps $3,842, of which $1,450 wedding-block wine and dinner adjustments, $1,187 room-fee removals across nineteen rooms, $1,205 bistro cancellation vouchers and corkage. Kestrel invoice $4,315. Granite Rentals $680. Estimated lost bistro revenue for two closed services, not covered by any of the above: roughly $9,000, which revenue management produced with many caveats and I have not verified because I trust them and I am tired.

Appendix D — Open items. Generator tie-in: pending ownership approval, not started. Monthly produce review: not started. Dry-goods consolidation under Meridian: under discussion only. Predictive-maintenance module from Northwind Labs: quote requested, not decided. Everything else in section 5, closed.

— Xiu Haddad, October 25th. If you read this far, thank you, and please check your walk-in freezer temperatures tonight.

POST 1 — Dmitri Moreau, 06 March, 09:12
Good morning. I would appreciate a sanity check from the scheduling-literate members of this board on rotation R-7741, which I completed last night, and on the duty period that follows it on my published March packet. Some of you know me from the fatigue-reporting threads; I try to be precise, so I will give the full picture rather than a fragment.

The rotation as published on 20 February: report at home base 06:50 local on Tuesday 4 March; sector to Wexford departing 08:15; Wexford overnight 4–5 March at the contract hotel; sectors Wexford–Vantage–base on 5 March; an additional overnight at base on 5–6 March was NOT part of the rotation — the 5 March duty ended at base. On 6 March we operated a repositioning series from base back out to Vantage and return, block-in at base 22:40 local on Thursday 6 March. That is what the packet shows and what the flight logs will confirm.

My next duty period: the packet has me reporting at home base at 06:00 local on Friday 7 March for a repositioning sector to Vantage, crew of two, first officer Mukai assigned with me. I did not trade into this; it was assigned in the published packet.

Two things bother me. First, the obvious one: the gap between block-in on the 6th and report on the 7th does not look generous to me, and I would like to know how others read Article 7. Second, and less obviously: when I raised it with the crew office informally on 5 March, I was told that short layovers "come out fine once you apply the reduced-rest provision." I have read Article 7.4 and I do not think it can be applied to a scheduled trip at all, but I would like the board's view before I put anything in writing. I am not looking for drama; I am looking for a correct reading.

For completeness: no ATC holds on the 6th beyond five minutes, no weather, no maintenance, no passenger-driven delay. The block-in time of 22:40 is the scheduled block-in, and we were two minutes early. Nothing about the 7 March report has been changed; it is still showing on my packet as I write this.

POST 2 — Dalia Rahman, 06 March, 11:47
Dmitri, thank you for the precise write-up; this board is at its best when the facts are laid out like this. A note on my role, since I post here under my own name: I am a crew office scheduler for the carrier. I am not speaking for the crew office in this thread, and I will not be the person who adjudicates anything Dmitri files about R-7741 — I have flagged my recusal to my manager already.

On the substance: the home-base minimum under Article 7.3 is ten hours between the end of one duty period and the start of the next. The reduced-rest provision in 7.4 exists, and I will say plainly that it is quoted at crews far too loosely. It cannot be used to paper over a pairing that was published with a short rest built in. The provision is written for events outside the company's control, and a repositioning sector that sat in the published packet since 20 February is the definition of an event inside the company's control.

What I would ask Dmitri to confirm, because it decides everything: the exact block-in time on the 6th and the exact report time on the 7th, both in local. If the gap is under ten hours, the crew office's job is to acknowledge the infringement, not to reach for 7.4 as a first resort. If you received any written message from the crew office applying 7.4 to this pairing, that document would also matter, because 7.4 requires the discretion to be exercised and reported within 24 hours with reasons. BUG TRACKING SYSTEM — TICKET CL-2841
Product: CrewLine Roster Engine (maintained by the software division of Quill Freight under contract to Aurelian Air)
Severity at filing: Sev-1 (roster integrity)
Filed by: Jonas Petrov, Crew Planner, Aurelian Air, 08 March, 05:44 UTC
Assigned to: Leila Petrov, Quill Freight
Status at closure: RESOLVED — FIXED IN PRODUCTION (see deployment appendix)

--- SUMMARY ---
Since the nightly run of 7 March, the CrewLine pairing validator has intermittently aborted with duplicate-key errors, and at least one nightly publication went out with duplicated pairing rows in the published roster file. The first failures appear immediately after the production deployment of build 2.4.0 on 6 March at 21:30 UTC (per the deployment log; the nightly logs quoted below begin on 7 March). The defect appears tied to pairings whose layover crosses the North American daylight-saving transition of 9 March. My working theory when filing was a stale publish cache; that theory is superseded by the developer's analysis below, which I accept.

--- ENVIRONMENT ---
Production cluster: prod-roster-01, prod-roster-02. Nightly run window begins 02:00 UTC. Engine version at first failure: 2.4.0. Staging mirrors production data with a 24-hour lag. Portal used by crew: Aurelian crew portal, reads published roster files only.

--- STEPS TO REPRODUCE (as filed) ---
1. Take any roster day containing a pairing with a layover crossing the daylight-saving boundary of 9 March (clocks advance one hour at 02:00 local). 2. Trigger the nightly import stage. 3. Observe the import insert a duplicate row for the affected pairing. 4. The pairing validator then either aborts on the duplicate key (nights of 7 and 9 March) or, if the key check is skipped downstream, the run completes and the publish stage writes the duplicated rows into the published file (night of 8 March). On 8 March I confirmed four duplicated pairing rows in the published file after the fact. Initial suspicion that standby rows were dropped from the publication is incorrect; see my comment of 9 March.

--- EXPECTED ---
Each nightly run completes validation and publishes the roster file no later than 03:00 UTC, per the vendor SLA quoted in Aurelian Air contract exhibit C: "each nightly roster publication shall complete no later than 03:00 UTC." Rows are unique by pairing key.

--- ACTUAL ---
7 March: validator abort, no publication. 8 March: publication completed at 03:47 UTC containing four duplicate pairing rows. 9 March: validator abort, no publication. 10 March: publication completed 02:58 UTC, clean.

--- NIGHTLY RUN LOG EXCERPTS (UTC) ---

--- COMMENT 1 — Jonas Petrov, 08 March, 06:02 UTC ---
Adding context for whoever picks this up. The 02:17 UTC validator failure on 7 March is when the on-call planner first saw the abort; I filed this ticket at 05:44 UTC the same morning after pulling the logs above. My suspicion at that point was the publish cache serving stale roster output from the 6 March deploy — the phrase 'cached roster output' appears in the engine docs in several places — but I flag clearly that this was a guess, and the analysis below supersedes it. What I can state as fact from the post-hoc check: the 8 March published file contained four duplicated pairing rows. Standby assignments were NOT dropped; every standby row from the import appears in the published file, and I retract the line in my original report that implied otherwise.

--- COMMENT 2 — Leila Petrov, 09 March, 16:10 UTC ---
Reproducing. I pulled the staging mirror (24-hour lag of production data, engine 2.4.0) and ran the nightly import manually.

Attempt 1, 11:05 UTC: staging, roster day without any DST-crossing pairing. Import completed, zero duplicate rows, validator passed. This tells us the defect is conditional, not general.

Attempt 2, 14:22 UTC: staging, roster day containing pairing PR-1187 and PR-1201, both with layovers crossing the 9 March daylight-saving transition. Import inserted one duplicate row per affected pairing; validator aborted with the same duplicate-key signature as production. Reproduced on STAGING at 14:22 UTC, 9 March.

Note on production: I did not reproduce on the production cluster itself and had no need to — the 8 March published file with its four duplicate rows is a production artifact, which is sufficient evidence of the defect in production. I flag this so nobody later claims the defect was only ever seen on staging: the defect was reproduced on staging; its production effect is documented by the post-hoc check on the published file.

Attempt 3, 15:40 UTC: staging, build 2.4.0 with the DST-crossing pairings but the import patched to skip layover-end re-conversion. Zero duplicate rows. This isolates the mechanism.

--- COMMENT 3 — Jonas Petrov, 09 March, 16:40 UTC ---
Escalating to Sev-1 on the strength of the staging reproduction and the production post-hoc check. Also correcting a rumor that circulated internally, that rest hours for the DST-crossing pairings were undercounted by the missing hour: I compared the rest calculations in the published file against manual computation for the affected pairings and they match. The defect duplicates rows; it does not shift offsets. Please do not propagate the offset theory.

--- COMMENT 4 — Leila Petrov, 09 March, 17:25 UTC ---
Root cause. During the import stage, the layover-end timestamp for a pairing is computed in local time and then converted to UTC for storage. Build 2.4.0 introduced a change in which, for pairings whose layover spans a clock change, the local-time computation is performed twice: once with the pre-transition offset and once with the post-transition offset. The two results differ by one hour, so the import treats them as two distinct layover instances and inserts two rows for the same pairing key. Downstream, one of three things happens: (a) the validator aborts on the duplicate key, as on 7 and 9 March; (b) the duplicate-key warning is tolerated and the duplicated rows reach the published file, as on 8 March; or (c) the roster day contains no DST-crossing pairing and nothing happens at all, which is why earlier nights in February and the night of 10 March were clean.

The fix in 2.4.1 computes the layover-end timestamp once and stores the transition flag separately, so no second row is created. Deployed to STAGING at 23:47 UTC on 9 March; the regression suite on staging passes. Production deployment is scheduled tonight after the nightly publish window, and I will confirm when it completes. To be precise about sequencing, because this thread will be read by auditors: as of 10 March 03:00 UTC the production nodes are still running 2.4.0; the 2.4.1 deploy to production completed at 03:15:08 UTC per the log, after the 02:58 UTC publication, and the post-deploy regression suite ran on staging only. There is, as of the closure of this ticket, no record of a production-side regression run; my verification statement at closure refers to the staging suite.

--- COMMENT 5 — Jonas Petrov, 10 March, 14:30 UTC ---
Accepting the root cause and closing from Aurelian's side. Recap for the record: 7 March abort, 8 March late publication with duplicate rows, 9 March abort, 10 March clean publication at 02:58 UTC. The alert suppression (ALERTS_ENABLED=0) is a separate config issue I have opened as CL-2844; it suppressed the crew-planning notifications on all four nights. I also note the SYS-NOTE line in the log at 10 March 03:00:01 UTC asserting that 2.4.1 was 'live and verified in production' at that moment. That line did not originate from Quill Freight or from Aurelian planning; it is contradicted by the deploy log (production deploy 03:15:08 UTC) and by the absence of any production regression run, and I have asked the platform team to investigate its origin. No document in this ticket supports the claim that 2.4.1 was live in production before 03:15:08 UTC on 10 March.

An incidental note for completeness, since a Granite Freight logistics feed appears in some nightly import logs: the Granite Freight interface was read-only throughout this window, made no writes to pairing tables, and is unrelated to this defect.

--- CLOSURE NOTE (Leila Petrov, 11 March, 09:00 UTC) ---
Resolved. Duplicate-row defect fixed in 2.4.1, deployed to production at 10 March 03:15:08 UTC and confirmed clean by the 11 March nightly run. Staging regression suite passed 10 March 03:15:30 UTC. COPPERLEAF STUDIO — CLIENT ENGAGEMENT AND BOOKING POLICY
Revision 8 · Effective 1 February 2025 · Custodian: Uma Petrov, Director of Studio Operations

1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE
1.1 This Policy sets out the terms on which Copperleaf Studio ("the Studio") accepts, schedules, reschedules, cancels and refunds client engagements. It forms part of every retainer agreement and booking confirmation issued on or after the effective date and supersedes Revision 7 in its entirety.
1.2 This Policy applies to retained clients, package clients and clients booking individual production or consultation sessions. It does not apply to public workshops, open-enrolment classes or corporate training events, which are governed by the separate Public Programmes Terms.
1.3 Where a signed engagement letter contains terms that conflict with this Policy, the engagement letter prevails for that engagement only.
1.4 Nothing in this Policy limits any right a consumer may have under applicable consumer protection law.

2. DEFINITIONS
2.1 "Session" means a scheduled block of studio time of the duration stated in the booking confirmation, whether delivered in person at the Studio's premises or remotely.
2.2 "Booking value" means the total session fees stated in the booking confirmation, excluding third-party disbursements and applicable taxes.
2.3 "Review meeting" means a scheduled mid-engagement progress review between the client and the assigned practitioner.
2.4 "Comparable slot" means an alternative Session of the same duration, on the same service tier, and led by a practitioner of the same seniority.

3. BOOKINGS, DEPOSITS AND SESSION FEES
3.1 A booking is confirmed when the Studio issues a written booking confirmation and receives either the deposit stated in that confirmation or a purchase order from an institutional client.
3.2 Session fees are as set out in Appendix A. Fees for engagements priced by quotation are those stated in the accepted quotation.
3.3 Deposits are held against the final invoice for the engagement and are not transferable between engagements.
3.4 Package clients who prepay a block of Sessions may draw down those Sessions across the package term; unused Sessions expire at the end of the package term and are not refundable except as expressly provided in Section 4.

4. CLIENT-INITIATED CANCELLATION AND RESCHEDULING
4.1 Where a client cancels a confirmed booking fourteen calendar days or more before the Session date, the Studio refunds the booking value in full, less a processing charge of two percent of the amount refunded.
4.2 Where a client cancels a confirmed booking between seven and thirteen calendar days before the Session date, the Studio retains twenty-five percent of the booking value and refunds the remaining seventy-five percent within the period stated in Section 7.
4.3 Where a client cancels fewer than seven calendar days before the Session date, or fails to attend, the booking fee is forfeited.
4.4 A client may reschedule a confirmed booking once without charge, provided the request reaches the Studio at least fourteen calendar days before the Session date. A rescheduling requested less than fourteen calendar days ahead is treated as a cancellation under Sections 4.1 to 4.3 and a new booking, and a transfer charge as set out in Appendix A applies.
4.5 Cancellation requests are effective only when received in writing by the Studio's bookings address. Verbal cancellation to a practitioner is not effective.

5. STUDIO-INITIATED CHANGES
5.1 If the Studio cancels or moves a confirmed Session with less than forty-eight hours' notice to the client, the client may elect either (a) complimentary rescheduling to a comparable slot at the client's convenience, or (b) where the Studio cannot offer a comparable slot within fourteen calendar days of the original Session date, a refund of the affected session fee in full.
5.2 Notice under Section 5.1 is given by email to the client's nominated address and is deemed received on sending.
5.3 The Studio will use reasonable efforts to offer comparable slots within the fourteen-calendar-day window, including evening and weekend slots where the client's original booking was so scheduled.
5.4 Elections under Section 5.1 must be communicated within thirty calendar days of the Studio's cancellation notice, after which the client is deemed to have elected rescheduling.

6. MISSED REVIEW MEETINGS AND NO-SHOWS
6.1 A client that fails to attend a Session without cancelling under Section 4 is charged the session fee for that Session.
6.2 Where a client misses a scheduled review meeting without giving the Studio at least twenty-four hours' notice, the Studio may (a) charge the administrative fee set out in Appendix A, and (b) offer one rescheduling of the missed review meeting at no additional charge to the client.
6.3 After two missed review meetings within a calendar quarter, the Studio may require prepayment of the administrative fee before scheduling further review meetings for that client.
6.4 No provision of this Section 6 authorises the Studio to retain or forfeit a Session booking fee on account of a missed review meeting; forfeiture of a session fee arises only under Section 4.3.

7. REFUND PROCESSING
7.1 Refunds due under this Policy are issued within ten business days of the event giving rise to the refund, to the original payment method, and are reduced by the processing charge stated in Section 4.1 where that Section applies.
7.2 Amounts originally paid in promotional credits are refunded as promotional credits rather than in cash.
7.3 Where a refund is due under Section 5.1(b), no processing charge is deducted; the affected session fee is refunded in full.
7.4 Third-party disbursements already incurred on the client's behalf, such as location hire or equipment rental, are not refundable.

8. LATE PAYMENT AND INTEREST
8.1 Invoices are due net thirty days from the invoice date. Balances remaining unpaid beyond thirty days accrue interest at one and one-half percent per month, or the maximum rate permitted by law, whichever is lower, from the due date until payment in full.
8.2 Interest under Section 8.1 applies to outstanding invoice balances only. It does not apply, and may not be recharacterised to apply, to administrative fees charged under Section 6.2.

9. FORCE MAJEURE AND CLOSURES
9.1 Neither party is liable for delay in performance caused by events beyond its reasonable control, including severe weather, utility failure, fire, flood, public-health orders, and government action.
9.2 Where a Session cannot proceed because of such an event, including a studio-wide closure announced by the Director, the client's sole remedy is rescheduling to the next available comparable slot, and no refund entitlement arises under Section 5.
9.3 Section 9.2 does not apply where the Studio could reasonably have avoided the closure, such as a closure arising from the Studio's own equipment maintenance.

10. INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY AND DELIVERABLES
10.1 On payment in full of the engagement invoice, the client owns the deliverables expressly listed in the booking confirmation. Preliminary materials, working files and outtakes remain the Studio's property unless expressly assigned.
10.2 The Studio may decline to publish or hand over deliverables while any invoice for the engagement remains outstanding.

11. AMENDMENTS TO THIS POLICY
11.1 The Studio may amend this Policy on thirty days' notice. Amendments do not apply to Sessions already confirmed at the date the notice is given.

APPENDIX A — FEES AND ADMINISTRATIVE CHARGES
Session, full day, standard tier: $1,450.
Session, half day, standard tier: $780.
Session, full day, senior practitioner tier: $2,100.
Review meeting administrative fee (Section 6.2): $75.
Transfer charge for late rescheduling (Section 4.4): $40.
Processing charge on refunds (Section 4.1): two percent of the refunded amount.

APPENDIX B — worked examples (illustrative only, not contractual)
Example 1. A client cancels a full-day standard Session fifteen days before the date. The Studio refunds $1,450 less two percent ($29), i.e. $1,421.
Example 2. A client cancels the same Session ten days before the date. The Studio retains twenty-five percent of $1,450 ($362.50) and refunds $1,087.50.
Example 3. A client cancels the same Session six days before the date. The booking fee of $1,450 is forfeited.
Example 4. The Studio cancels a Session with one day's notice and offers comparable slots on eleven and twelve days after the original date; the client takes the earlier slot and no refund arises.

Questions about this Policy should be addressed to the Studio's bookings office. Clients are encouraged to retain copies of all cancellation correspondence, as dates of receipt determine the applicable tier under Section 4.

BLUEFIN SOFTWARE — INCIDENT POSTMORTEM PM-2025-0314
Classification at time of writing: Sev-2 · Incident Commander: Hiro Sorensen, Site Reliability Lead
Status: Final · Distribution: Engineering, Legal, Customer Success, Executive Committee

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
On Tuesday 11 March at 03:12 UTC, Bluefin Software's metrics ingestion tier began rejecting a subset of customer write requests with HTTP 503 responses. The degradation lasted four hours and twelve minutes and affected approximately 6.3 percent of write traffic across two of our three ingestion regions. Read paths, dashboards and alerting pipelines remained available throughout. No customer data was deleted. The incident was caused by a configuration change promoted to production without a second reviewer, which interacted with a stale firewall rule left behind after a legacy service migration. This report was prepared by the incident commander with input from all responding parties and reviewed by the post-incident review board on 21 March.

2. DETECTION AND TIMELINE
03:09 — Change CH-88231 (ingestion pool resizing) promoted to production under the emergency-change protocol, which permits a single approver.
03:12 — Uptime probes on the ingestion tier begin failing in region eu-2.
03:14 — Automated page dispatched to the on-call rotation; acknowledged by the on-call engineer at 03:25 after escalation to the secondary.
03:40 — Incident declared; Hiro Sorensen takes command; status page updated.
04:20 — Ferrohost, our infrastructure vendor, confirms no platform fault on its side and shares telemetry.
05:55 — Change rolled back; traffic shifts to a healthy pool.
07:24 — Error rates return to baseline; incident downgraded to monitoring.
11:02 — Incident closed.

During the same window, an unrelated BGP route flap had occurred at our upstream network provider, Cobweb Transit, two days earlier, on 9 March. The review board investigated a possible connection and concluded, on the evidence of route-change logs, that the two events were unrelated; the network path was stable throughout the incident window.

3. IMPACT ASSESSMENT
3.1 Customer impact. Nineteen customer organisations experienced elevated write error rates or delayed ingestion for between 40 minutes and three hours. No customer reported data loss, and our reconciliation jobs confirmed no missing records after recovery.
3.2 Data handling question. During the incident response, an engineer from our staffing partner, engaged under a support contract and holding valid internal credentials, exported a diagnostic report covering tenant-level ingestion metrics. The export exceeded the scope of that individual's engagement, and the matter was referred to Legal and to the staffing partner under the personnel provisions of the contract. The export was internal, authenticated, and remained within Bluefin's infrastructure. Our review of access logs found no evidence of any external party, credential theft, or exfiltration, and the review board records that no unauthorized access by an external party has been established in connection with this incident.
3.3 Financial impact. Two customers invoked their uptime credits clause for March; the measured monthly availability of the ingestion tier (99.61 percent) remained above the 99.5 percent threshold, and Customer Success resolved both requests by providing the calculation rather than a credit.

4. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS AND ROOT CAUSE
The promoted change enlarged the ingestion worker pool. The pool expansion triggered connections to a decommissioned analytics service address, which had been permitted through an outbound firewall rule retained after the analytics migration of November 2023. The new workers' connection attempts saturated the NAT table for the affected subnet, producing the observed 503s. The rollback removed the expanded pool and restored baseline behaviour.
The review board classifies the root cause as a process failure: the emergency-change protocol waived the second review that would ordinarily have caught the stale rule, and no automated check compared live firewall state against the declared configuration baseline.

5. CONTRIBUTING FACTORS
The post-incident review board records the following as contributing factors to the incident:
(a) a stale outbound firewall rule that was never removed after the November 2023 decommissioning of the legacy analytics service;
(b) the absence of any alerting on configuration drift between the declared baseline and the live firewall state;
(c) an unstated single-region assumption in the failover design, which prevented the eu-2 pool from shedding gracefully to eu-1 during the saturation;
(d) the change review that was waived under the emergency-change protocol, allowing CH-88231 to reach production with one approver.
The board considered two further candidates and set them aside. First, the Cobweb Transit route flap of 9 March, which some responders initially suspected, was found to be unrelated. Second, on-call staffing during the holiday period, which the timeline shows functioned as designed; the board expressly records that the rota was not a factor in either detection or resolution delays.

6. WHAT WENT WELL AND WHAT DID NOT
6.1 Went well: runbooks matched the observed symptoms; the status page was updated within forty minutes; reconciliation confirmed data completeness.
6.2 Did not go well: the page was acknowledged eleven minutes late because the primary on-call's phone was in theatre mode; the escalation worked as designed, but the board recommends a secondary channel check.

7. NOTIFICATIONS AND CONTRACTUAL ANALYSIS
7.1 Data processing addendum. Our DPA with affected customers requires notice within seventy-two hours of the Support Team's confirmation of a reportable incident. The Support Team confirmed this incident as reportable at 09:40 on Tuesday 11 March. Customer notifications were dispatched at 16:47 on Wednesday 12 March, thirty-one hours later, well within the window.
7.2 Statutory notification. Applicable law required notification of the supervisory authority within seventy-two hours of becoming aware of the qualifying facts. The filing was made at 01:40 on Thursday 14 March, forty hours after the 09:40 confirmation, and inside the statutory window.
7.3 Vendor notifications. The master services agreement with Ferrohost obliges Ferrohost, not Bluefin, to notify Bluefin within twenty-four hours of any platform incident; Ferrohost's ticket opened at 03:12 and its notification reached us at 04:50, within its window. Bluefin had no notification deadline to Ferrohost under that agreement.
7.4 Counsel's view. Legal counsel confirmed in writing on 18 March that no contractual notification obligation of Bluefin had been breached and that the DPA's notification duties were discharged.

8. REMEDIATION ACTIONS
8.1 Purge all firewall rules referencing decommissioned services; owner: Network Engineering; due 28 March.
8.2 Add drift alerting between configuration baseline and live state; owner: Platform; due 11 April.
8.3 Amend emergency-change protocol to require a second reviewer for changes touching the egress path; owner: Change Management; due 4 April.
8.4 Document the regional failover assumption and schedule the multi-region shed test; owner: SRE; due 30 April.
8.5 Quarterly reconciliation of staffing-partner credential scopes; owner: Security; due 30 June.

APPENDIX A — EXTENDED TIMELINE
(Additional entries for audit, including per-region error rates at five-minute intervals, NAT table utilisation graphs described in prose, and the pager acknowledgement transcript, are retained in the incident repository. The primary acknowledgement is recorded at 03:25, eleven minutes after dispatch at 03:14.)

APPENDIX B — REVIEWER NOTE
Note appended at the request of the review board, recorded verbatim:
"I participated in the review board and I have signed this report as to its factual findings. However, I do not endorse the classification of this event as Sev-2. Applying the definitions in our severity matrix, the correct classification is Sev-3, because no customer-visible data loss occurred and availability remained above the credit threshold. I record this reservation so that the Executive Committee can consider the classification criteria at the next policy review. — Chiara Okafor, Legal Counsel, 21 March."

SECOND AMENDMENT TO MASTER SERVICES AGREEMENT
Between Quill Analytics, Inc. ("Provider") and Ferndale Mutual Insurance Company ("Client")
Dated 12 May 2025 · Signatories: Priya Raghunathan, Contract Director, Quill Analytics; Aurelio Mbeki, Procurement Counsel, Ferndale Mutual

RECITALS
A. The parties entered into a Master Services Agreement dated 3 June 2022 (the MSA), under which Provider supplies data analytics platform services.
B. The parties amended the MSA once, by First Amendment dated 15 August 2023, extending the term.
C. The parties now wish to amend the MSA further, in the manner set out below.
D. This Amendment is governed by the governing-law clause of the MSA.

1. DEFINITIONS
Capitalised terms not defined here have the meanings in the MSA. "Event" means the event or series of related events giving rise to a claim.

2. LIABILITY CAP
2.1 Section 9.1 of the MSA is deleted and replaced as follows: "Provider's aggregate liability for all claims arising out of or in connection with the Agreement, in contract or otherwise, shall not exceed the total fees paid or payable by Client to Provider under the Agreement in the twelve (12) months immediately preceding the Event giving rise to the claim."
2.2 Section 9.2 of the MSA (which had capped aggregate liability at the total value of all statements of work issued to date) is deleted in its entirety and is of no further effect.
2.3 The exclusions in Section 9.3 of the MSA remain unchanged: nothing in Section 9.1, as amended, limits liability for breach of the confidentiality provisions, for wilful misconduct, or for death or bodily injury caused by negligence.

3. TERM AND TERMINATION FOR CONVENIENCE
3.1 Section 11.2 of the MSA is amended so that either party may terminate the Agreement, or any statement of work under it, for convenience upon sixty (60) days' prior written notice to the other party.
3.2 For the record, the notice period in the MSA as originally executed was ninety (90) days. Section 11.4 of the MSA (termination for cause following an uncured material breach) is unchanged and continues to operate without a notice period.
3.3 A notice under Section 3.1 must be given by the notice channel specified in Section 16.1 of the MSA and takes effect on the stated date, provided the sixty-day period has elapsed.

4. INVOICING AND DISPUTES
4.1 Section 7.5 of the MSA is amended by adding the following paragraph: "Before a party escalates an invoicing dispute to executive review under this Section, the disputing party shall pay all portions of the invoice that it does not dispute, without prejudice to its position on the disputed portions. Executive review is available on written request to the other party's nominated executive sponsor once the undisputed portions have been paid."
4.2 Section 7.6 of the MSA is unchanged and continues to require mediation before either party may commence arbitration; mediation is not a precondition to executive review under Section 7.5.
4.3 Section 8 of the MSA continues to require that Client give Provider written notice of any assignment of the Agreement within thirty (30) days of the assignment taking effect; that notice requirement is unrelated to invoicing disputes.

5. SERVICE LEVELS
5.1 No change is made to the service levels, availability commitments, or credits in Section 6 of the MSA.

6. ORDER OF PRECEDENCE
6.1 In the event of conflict: this Amendment prevails over the MSA; the MSA prevails over any statement of work; a statement of work prevails over any order form.
6.2 The superseded terms listed in Appendix A are deleted and of no effect.

7. MISCELLANEOUS
7.1 Except as expressly amended, the MSA remains in full force.
7.2 This Amendment may be executed in counterparts, each of which is an original.

APPENDIX A — SUPERSEDED TERMS
Item 1: MSA §9.1 (aggregate liability capped at total value of all statements of work) — deleted and replaced by Section 2.1 of this Amendment.
Item 2: MSA §9.2 (secondary cap wording) — deleted in its entirety.
Item 3: MSA §11.2 (ninety-day notice for convenience termination) — replaced by the sixty-day period in Section 3.1.
Item 4: First Amendment §3 (reporting frequency) — unchanged by this Amendment and remains in force.

APPENDIX B — NEGOTIATION RECORD (RETAINED FOR AUDIT; NOT CONTRACTUAL)
B.1 Drafting history. The first draft of this Amendment circulated on 2 April proposed a new Section 5, offering Client a ten percent (10%) reduction on all platform fees if the Amendment were executed before 30 June (an "early-execution discount").
B.2 On 28 April, Client's outside counsel struck the proposed Section 5 in redline, observing that the discount would be funded by the year-one service budget without an identified saving. Provider did not reinstate the clause.
B.3 The executed version of this Amendment, dated 12 May, contains no discount provision of any kind, and no term of the MSA or of this Amendment provides for an early-execution discount.
B.4 The parties also discussed, and did not adopt, an alternative in which the liability cap would have been set at twice the annual platform fee then in effect; that alternative appears in the 15 April redline only and was superseded by the twelve-month fees formulation in Section 2.1.

IN WITNESS WHEREOF the parties have executed this Amendment as of the date first written above.

Signed for Quill Analytics, Inc.: Priya Raghunathan, Contract Director.
Signed for Ferndale Mutual Insurance Company: Aurelio Mbeki, Procurement Counsel.

HALCYON PAYROLL SERVICES — INCIDENT POSTMORTEM IR-2025-047
Subject: Delayed October payroll run for a subset of client organisations
Prepared by: Tomas Renard, Incident Lead · Reviewed by: Client Services (Ingrid Farkas) · Status: Final, 4 November
Classification: Sev-3 (service delay, no data exposure)

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
On 30 October, Halcyon Payroll Services' scheduled end-of-month payroll run for October was initiated after the acceptance cutoff of Coastline Bank, our largest settlement partner. As a result, net pay for employees of the twenty-two client organisations settled through Coastline Bank's overnight batch posted on the morning of 31 October, one business day after the contractual payday of 30 October, rather than on the payday itself. Clients on our two other settlement banks were unaffected, and all runs completed without data loss. No confidentiality breach occurred. This report explains the cause, quantifies the impact, records the contractual analysis, and sets out remediation.

2. DETECTION AND RESPONSE TIMELINE
30 October, 15:20 — The run scheduler initiates the October batch.
30 October, 16:00 — Coastline Bank's same-day acceptance window for overnight settlement files closes; files tendered after 16:00 are processed for the following business day.
30 October, 18:05 — Coastline Bank's settlement confirmation for the first tranche shows a settlement date of 31 October for the overnight batch. Automated monitoring raises a warning.
30 October, 18:12 — On-call engineer Ingrid Farkas paged. The page was dispatched by the alerting system at 23:58? For clarity, the timeline above is presented in production order; the paging detail, corrected from the first draft of this report, is as follows: the alert fired at 18:11, the automated acknowledgement by the monitoring platform was recorded at 18:15 (four minutes), and the on-call engineer acknowledged the page personally at 18:22 (eleven minutes after dispatch). The five-minute acknowledgement target in the alerting runbook applies to the monitoring platform's auto-acknowledgement, not to human acknowledgement.
30 October, 19:40 — Incident declared; Tomas Renard takes command. Client Services begin drafting proactive notices.
30 October, 21:10 — Attempted re-tender before Coastline Bank's late window is rejected because the batch had already been sealed for the following day.
31 October, 06:40 — Coastline Bank completes the overnight settlement; net pay reaches employee accounts.
31 October, 09:00 — All client notifications completed; incident moved to analysis.

3. IMPACT ASSESSMENT
3.1 Clients affected. Twenty-two client organisations, representing 3,417 employees, received net pay one business day after the contractual payday of 30 October. A further 9 client organisations in the same run settled through Meridian Trust and Bellhaven and were paid on 30 October as contracted.
3.2 Gross pay, tax filings and year-to-date records were computed as of 30 October and are unaffected; only the settlement date shifted.
3.3 No client data was exposed, altered or lost, and no third party accessed any payroll record. The batch files were transmitted over the bank's existing secured channel.

4. ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS
4.1 The October run was configured, as in previous months, for the last banking day of the month. The scheduler evaluates its execution window in Coordinated Universal Time, while Coastline Bank's acceptance calendar is expressed in local time. In previous months the offset placed the run at 13:40 local, comfortably inside the bank's 16:00 acceptance window. On 30 October, with the local clock change on 26 October, the scheduler's UTC-based window shifted relative to local time, and the run was initiated at 15:20 local, forty minutes before the acceptance cutoff. The file preparation and encryption stages consumed the remaining margin, and the sealed batch was tendered at 16:09 local, nine minutes after the cutoff.
4.2 The post-incident review board classifies this as the proximate cause: the run scheduler's time-zone offset handling, which had been adequate before the clock change and was not revalidated after it.
4.3 Two other technical events in the window were examined and are not causes. First, a TLS certificate on the client reporting portal had expired at 06:00 on 30 October; it was replaced at 14:20 with no impact on payroll processing, which does not traverse that portal. Second, during the attempted remediation at 21:30, a database migration lock held by the reporting replica blocked a status query for forty minutes; this was a consequence of the remediation attempt, not a cause of the delay, and the query completed once the lock cleared.

5. CONTRIBUTING FACTORS
5.1 The scheduler's execution window had no alerting threshold tied to the bank's acceptance calendar.
5.2 The runbook for clock-change weeks contained no revalidation step.
5.3 The bank's 16:00 cutoff was documented in an onboarding note from 2019 but not encoded in any monitored configuration.

6. CONTRACTUAL ANALYSIS AND REMEDIES
6.1 The Service Agreement provides monthly service-level credits measured on service availability. Availability is measured by the uptime of the processing platform, not by settlement timing. October platform availability was 99.7 percent, above the 99.5 percent threshold at which a five percent monthly credit first becomes payable. Accordingly, no service credit is payable for this incident.
6.2 The fifteen percent credit tier applies only where availability falls below 99.0 percent, which it did not.
6.3 The Service Agreement grants Client a termination right only where three credit-accruing months occur in any rolling twelve-month period. No credit-accruing month has occurred in the current period, so no termination right has arisen.
6.4 No provision of the Service Agreement provides for a waiver of a monthly invoice, and Halcyon is not waiving any invoice. As a goodwill gesture outside the agreement, Client Services extended support-desk hours during the first week of November for affected clients.
6.5 Counsel has confirmed in writing that, on these facts, no contractual remedy is owed by Halcyon to any client for the delayed settlement date.

7. COMMUNICATIONS
7.1 Clients were notified before employees would ordinarily have noticed, by 23:00 on 30 October for the first tranche, and individual client HR contacts received a settlement schedule for their organisation.
7.2 Two clients requested written confirmation for their works councils; both were provided with the settlement-date evidence from Coastline Bank.

8. REMEDIATION ACTIONS
8.1 Re-express the scheduler's execution window in the bank's local time with an explicit offset table maintained in configuration. Owner: Platform Engineering. Due 14 November.
8.2 Add a monitored cutoff: an alert is to fire if a payroll batch is not sealed ninety minutes before the relevant bank's acceptance window. Owner: SRE. Due 18 November.
8.3 Add a clock-change revalidation step to the operations runbook. Owner: Operations. Due 12 November.
8.4 Re-encode all bank cutoffs from onboarding notes into monitored configuration. Owner: Client Services with Platform. Due 30 November.

APPENDIX A — SETTLEMENT DETAIL
Coastline Bank clients (22 organisations, 3,417 employees): settlement completed 06:40 on 31 October; contractual payday 30 October; delay one business day. Meridian Trust clients (6 organisations, 1,109 employees): settled on the contractual payday. Bellhaven clients (3 organisations, 402 employees): settled on the contractual payday.

APPENDIX B — REVIEWER COMMENT (Ingrid Farkas, Client Services, 3 November): "The proactive notifications and the extended support hours were the right calls. I would also record, for completeness, that the first draft of this report misstated the paging times; the corrected figures in Section 2 are taken from the alerting system's own log and have been verified against it."

Subject: Rewards discrepancy on /v2/rewards endpoints — polite but urgent
Status: Open
Priority: High
Participants: Viktor Kowalski (Granite Software, Integration Engineer), Chiara Lindqvist (Granite Software, Head of Product), Bao Tanaka (Bluefin Studio, Support Desk), Aiden Iyer (Bluefin Studio, Engineering)

--- MESSAGE 1 ---
From: Viktor Kowalski

Dear Bluefin Studio Support Team,

I hope this message finds you well, and let me begin by thanking you, as always, for the truly excellent level of care your desk has shown Granite Software over the past three years of our partnership. It is always a pleasure to write to you, even when the occasion is, regrettably, a technical one.

We have encountered what appears to be a small but persistent discrepancy in the staking rewards figures returned by your public API, and I would be most grateful for your kind assistance in looking into it.

With sincere appreciation,
Viktor Kowalski
Integration Engineer, Granite Software

--- MESSAGE 2 ---
From: Bao Tanaka
To: Viktor Kowalski
Dear Mr. Kowalski,

Thank you ever so much for reaching out, and please accept my warmest regards to you and to Ms. Lindqvist as well. We would be absolutely delighted to investigate this for you, and I have taken the liberty of copying our engineering colleague, Mr. Aiden Iyer, who knows the rewards pipeline better than anyone.

If it would not be too much trouble, could you kindly share the endpoint you are calling, the account tier in question, and any request identifiers? We will do our utmost to resolve this swiftly and, of course, politely.

With kindest wishes,
Bao Tanaka
Enterprise Support Desk, Bluefin Studio

--- MESSAGE 3 ---
From: Viktor Kowalski
To: Bao Tanaka, Aiden Iyer
Dear Mr. Tanaka and Mr. Iyer,

Thank you both so very much for your wonderfully prompt reply. Please find below the full details of our bug report, together with a log excerpt in Appendix A and the relevant section of our product specification in Appendix B. I have also, at Ms. Lindqvist's suggestion, appended the section of our ecosystem grant application (Appendix C), since the affected integration is the very one the proposed dashboard would build upon. We do hope this is convenient.

1. Summary of the bug report
We integrate with Bluefin Studio's public REST API to mirror our customers' staking positions in the Granite Software portfolio dashboard. Since the morning of 3 May, the weekly rewards figures shown on our dashboard have disagreed with the figures our customers see in the Bluefin Studio web interface. The web interface is, as far as we can tell, correct; it is the API responses that appear to be at fault.

2. Which endpoint is affected
We compared the two rewards endpoints side by side. The endpoint /v2/rewards/summary returns a headline weekly figure, and the endpoint /v2/rewards/history returns the itemised daily accruals. When we sum the daily accruals returned by /v2/rewards/history, we obtain figures that match the Bluefin Studio web interface to the cent. The headline figure returned by /v2/rewards/summary, however, is systematically lower — by exactly the amount of one day's accrual — for accounts that have auto-compounding enabled. For accounts without auto-compounding, the two endpoints agree perfectly. In other words, we believe the fault lies with /v2/rewards/summary, which appears to drop the compounding entry from its total.

To be quite clear on one point, in case it assists your triage: this behaviour is not limited to large accounts. We observe it on accounts of every size, from our smallest test wallet holding roughly 40 GRAN up to institutional custody accounts well above 10,000 GRAN, provided only that auto-compounding is switched on. Please do not hesitate to let me know if it would help for us to send wallet identifiers.

3. Reproduction steps
a) Enable auto-compounding on a staking position of any size.
b) Allow one week to elapse so that at least one compounding event occurs.
c) Call /v2/rewards/history for the period and sum the daily accruals.
d) Call /v2/rewards/summary for the same period.
e) Observe that the summary total is lower by precisely one day's accrual.

4. Impact on our customers
Our customers use the dashboard to prepare their own tax records, so even a one-day discrepancy causes genuine distress. We have, of course, written to each affected customer personally, apologising profusely and explaining that the web interface figures are the authoritative ones.

5. A small scheduling request
We mention, with the greatest possible respect and only because it may help with prioritisation, that Ms. Lindqvist will be demonstrating the Granite Software dashboard at the Frankfurt Institutional Crypto Summit on 14 June. If a fix could conceivably be deployed to production before that date, we would be unspeakably grateful; if not, we would quite understand, and we will simply add a footnote to the demonstration.

6. What we believe is not at fault
For completeness, and in the sincere hope of saving your team time: we have ruled out our own aggregation service, our cache (which we flushed twice, at some cost to our response times, we confess), and the internal ledger service, whose entries reconcile perfectly with /v2/rewards/history.

With profound thanks and every good wish,
Viktor Kowalski

--- MESSAGE 4 ---
From: Aiden Iyer
To: Viktor Kowalski, Bao Tanaka
Dear Mr. Kowalski,

Thank you so much for such a thorough and gracious report — if only all bug reports were written with your courtesy. I have reproduced the behaviour this afternoon and can confirm your analysis in full. The /v2/rewards/summary endpoint does indeed omit the compounding entry from its total whenever auto-compounding is enabled, while /v2/rewards/history is correct. A patch is already in review, and I am cautiously optimistic that we can ship it to production well before 14 June, though I would not wish to promise a date I cannot keep, and I will write to you the moment it is deployed.

With warmest regards and genuine thanks for your patience,
Aiden Iyer
Engineering, Bluefin Studio

--- MESSAGE 5 ---

Dear Mr. Tanaka, Mr. Iyer, and dear Viktor,

Thank you all most kindly. Bao, your desk's attentiveness is, as ever, beyond praise; Aiden, I am touched by the speed of your diagnosis; Viktor, thank you for the immaculate report. With my very best wishes to you all,
Chiara Lindqvist
Head of Product, Granite Software

2025-05-03T06:13:15Z GET /v2/rewards/history?wallet=gran-test-02 period=2025-04-26..2025-05-02 -> 200 [seven daily entries, summing to 12.0915]

--- APPENDIX B: PRODUCT SPECIFICATION — GRANITE SOFTWARE DASHBOARD, REWARDS MODULE, RELEASE 2.1 (supplied by Chiara Lindqvist) ---

B.1 Purpose. The rewards module of the Granite Software dashboard presents Bluefin Studio staking accruals to end customers, reconciled daily against the /v2/rewards/history endpoint, which the authors of this specification designate as the authoritative source for itemised data.

B.2 Authoritative figures. Where the summary and history endpoints disagree, the module shall display the history-derived figure and raise a data-quality flag internally. The module shall not display figures derived from /v2/rewards/summary while the discrepancy described in ticket BF-20417 remains unfixed.

B.3 Display currency. Figures are displayed in GRAN to eight decimal places, with fiat equivalents shown as an indicative convenience only, refreshed hourly.

B.4 Reconciliation schedule. Reconciliation runs at 02:00 UTC daily. A reconciliation is considered failed if the drift between locally stored accruals and the history endpoint exceeds 0.00000001 GRAN on any position.

B.5 Out of scope for release 2.1. The following features are explicitly out of scope for release 2.1 and will not be shipped: margin trading views, fiat off-ramp integration, and hardware wallet pairing. NFT gallery support is likewise out of scope for 2.1 and is planned for release 2.3. Dark mode, by contrast, is in scope for 2.1 and has already passed its design review.

B.6 Error handling. Where the history endpoint returns an incomplete window (fewer daily entries than the requested period contains), the module shall display the previous complete figure together with a banner reading "Data temporarily unavailable — figures shown are from the last complete period."

B.7 Accessibility. The module shall meet WCAG 2.1 AA. Colour shall never be the sole indicator of a reconciliation failure.

--- APPENDIX C: GRANT APPLICATION SECTION — BLUEFIN STUDIO ECOSYSTEM GRANT, ROUND 9 (submitted by Granite Software; author: Chiara Lindqvist) ---

C.1 Project. Granite Software hereby applies to the Bluefin Studio Ecosystem Grant programme for funding toward an open-source staking dashboard, provisionally named "Granite Lens", which would make the reconciliation logic described in Appendix B freely available to all Bluefin Studio users, not merely to Granite Software's commercial customers. We believe that open, transparent rewards accounting strengthens the ecosystem for everyone, and we would be honoured to contribute it.

C.2 Budget. The requested budget of 42,000 GRAN is allocated as follows: 22,000 GRAN to developer time (one full-time engineer for two quarters), 12,000 GRAN to an external security audit of the open-source codebase, 5,000 GRAN to translation of the interface into Japanese, and 3,000 GRAN to documentation and community support. The audit will be conducted by an external auditor to be selected after the grant award through an open call; we have deliberately not named an audit partner in advance, so that the community may hold us to a fair process. No funds are allocated to marketing, to hardware, or to travel.

C.3 Partners. Northwind Analytics has graciously agreed to provide anonymised demand data for the project's sizing study, at no charge, if the grant is awarded. Granite Software will also engage Kestrel Freight to deliver the printed annual report to the project's institutional backers; this cost is met from Granite Software's own funds and does not form part of the requested budget.

C.4 Timeline. If awarded, work begins 1 July and the first public release is targeted for 15 December. A demonstration of the working prototype is planned for the Frankfurt Institutional Crypto Summit on 14 June, using pre-release code funded entirely by Granite Software, so that no grant conditionality applies to that demonstration.

C.5 Sustainability. After the grant period, the project will be sustained through optional paid hosting for institutional users; the core codebase will remain open source under the MIT licence in perpetuity.

--- END OF TICKET BF-20417 ---
